records.text: EUR credit: Shrugging off headlines but demanding a higher new concession. EUR credit markets largely shrugged off the recent flare-up in geopolitical and tariff risks, with the main impact materializing in the primary market. EUR IG and HY secondary spreads widened by a mere 3-10bp at their peak, remaining near the tight end of their historical range. Even within indices, the flight-to-quality was modest, with BBBs slightly underperforming As and Bs slightly underperforming BBs, pointing to only a marginal repricing of growth risk (Exhibit 1). Further, country-level spread dispersion remained near historical lows, suggesting the market was skeptical of any meaningful, differentiated impact from the tariff headlines (Exhibit 2). The real impact, in our view, was felt on the issuance calendar. Primary market activity in the EUR IG market slowed to an average daily run rate of €2 billion this week, down from €7 billion in the two prior weeks. While some slowdown is typical after the heavy issuance of early January, the pressure was evident in new issue concessions, which picked up to 11bp on a two-week average basis, above the 6bp average last year (Exhibit 3 and 4). We expect this bout of volatility to subside and reiterate our recommendation to be long credit for carry while maintaining hedges against tail risks. In Argentina, economic activity was stagnant throughout 2025. We think this reflects (at least in part) an overvalued currency and represents a risk to the credibility of the FX regime, although these concerns are muted for the moment. As of November 2025, the monthly GDP proxy EMAE was unchanged versus December 2024. Construction is flat versus Q1 25 and manufacturing has declined 3%. Multiple factors help explain this weakness. The political uncertainty and election- related volatility experienced in 2025 are probably a relevant contributor. However, we believe this also reflects an overvalued currency. The multilateral REER is now only 6% weaker than in 2017, a year with a 4% primary deficit (vs 1.4% surplus in 2025) and much tighter credit spreads (the sovereign was at 350bp after the 2017 midterms, compared to 560bp now). Argentina was growing close to 3% annually back then. In this context, a weaker currency is needed to stimulate demand for non-tradables, import competing goods and exports with public spending and investment more depressed. Short-term, and assuming services provision is not disrupted, the cost of targeting services rather than retaliating more aggressively through goods would likely be smaller. records.text: 23 January 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 44 Deutsche Bank AG A glimmer of solace for OATs near-term The latest developments over Greenland have overshadowed the recent news flow surrounding France and PM Lecornu’s last attempt to pass the 2026 budget. As reported by the press, the latest budget concessions might be enough to secure the Socialists’ abstention during a crucial no confidence vote that is expected to follow the activation of Article 49.3, which bypasses the parliamentary vote process. At this stage we do not know the exact deficit target for 2026 which, according to the French PM, would be no higher than 5%. While these latest budget concessions might create upside risks to a 5% deficit target, it’s worth emphasizing that as far as trading of OATs is concerned, the avoidance of elections and the survival of the government are likely to matter more than a less ambitious deficit target, at least in the near-term. Hence, this is a net positive for OATs. The reason we believe this is the case has to do with current cheap OAT valuations vs fundamentals, an indication that a certain degree of political risk premium (cheapness) is embedded in OATs prices. The avoidance of elections should lead to a reduction of that risk premium, although we wouldn’t expect it to go to zero since the Presidential 2027 elections are looming. records.text: US Economics Weekly23 January 2026 ab 25 Tax refund tracking: withholding in line with 2025 The One Big Beautiful Bill Act implemented tax changes retroactive to 2025. That means individuals can claim refunds against their 2025 income when they file their 2025 tax returns in 2026. Because the tax law changes were passed midyear, most individuals were unlikely to fully account for the changes by adjusting their withheld income. As a result, we expect larger than normal tax refunds sent to households in 2026. We have seen a range of estimates for how strong the refund season might be this spring, from as low as $30 billion more than 2025 to as high as $100 billion. We suspect there may be other estimates even higher. We estimate refund checks to households $50 to $60 billion higher this year than last year. That could be right or wrong, but this is something we can track in real time from the Daily Treasury Statement. As shown in the two figures below, we can trace out the magnitude of refunds The top left shows the total dollar amount of refunds issued by the IRS, including both electronic and checks, and the top right hand side shows the outflow from Treasury for electronically transferred refunds. We show the response of the policy rate to shifts in the magnitude of a temporary deviation of inflation from target, and we do the same for shifts in the duration of a small inflation deviation (Exhibit 5). In each case, we report the implied peak policy change under a Taylor rule (light blue) and an optimal policy framework (dark blue). We see that the size of the policy response increases linearly with the magnitude of the shock. Policy is also incrementally more responsive when the inflation deviation becomes somewhat persistent (lasting 8 quarters instead of 4) than when the inflation deviation turns out to be very persistent (lasting 16 quarters instead of 12). In both cases, optimal policy is less reactive because it either anticipates the inflation deviation being temporary or is more reluctant to respond to small deviations. Optimal policy would therefore only respond by moving at least 50bp if a one-year inflation deviation is at least 0.6pp, or if a smaller 0.2pp deviation is sustained for more than two years. records.text: UK Economics 23 January 2026 Citi Research 2 Who is Andy Burnham? Andy Burnham is the current Mayor of Greater Manchester and one of the more popular figures in the Labour party. He was first elected as an MP in 2001 and has held various roles in both Government and opposition, which include jobs in the Department for Health, the Home Office, and the Treasury. He challenged for the Labour leadership in 2010 following the resignation of Gordon Brown, and then again when Ed Miliband resigned in 2015. He was elected as the Mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017, where he current serves. He has, over the last few months, been cited as a possible challenger for the Labour leadership. This speculation first picked up in September 2025 when the Starmer government faced a series of scandals ahead of the party conference.1 A recent resignation in the constituency of Gorton and Denton has led to a renewed interest in both whether Mr Burnham will challenge for the leadership and also what a Burnham Premiership may look like and its implications for markets. The Path to Power The path to the premiership is difficult. Leadership challenges have been an important, and recurring, theme in UK politics over the last ten years. The hearing on Governor Cook’s dismissal has reduced market‑implied probabilities of aggressive Fed cuts somewhat, although these have not been very high for a while. The options market has also started pricing in significant hike probabilities in 2027 and beyond, but payer skew on the left-hand side is still too cheap to fade these, in our view. Implied/realized ratios are still quite high even after this week moves and are at levels that are likely to reinforce short‑gamma selling. As a result, while short- expiry vol is unlikely to fall, there are few near-term catalysts for a spike. More importantly, there is some tentative evidence that the rise in labor market slack was not as severe as feared. The unemployment rate fell back to 4.375% in December from 4.5% in November (the latter was initially reported at 4.6%). In addition, the quits rate has risen and now looks stable for most o f the past 18 months. These data have not uniformly improved; job openings to unemployed has fallen and sentiment is substantially weaker. Nonetheless, we see reasons for some degree of greater optimism around the risk distribution for the labor market. records.text: ab 23 January 2026 Global Research US Economics Weekly A bumpy 2026 Economic Comment: a bumpy 2026 We kicked off 2026 with a comment titled "We expect a bumpy 2026." Optimism over the prospects for the US in 2026 appear both buoyant and pervasive. We expect fiscal policy and ongoing wealth effects to support decent growth too. However, that is not without risks. The breadth of expansion in the economy and the labor market has been quite weak. Expectations rest on fiscal stimulus, and thus far income tax withholding is merely tracking 2025. The pace of tech investment is already brisk and expected to build on that high base, while the related equity valuations drive the consumption growth in the economy, disproportionately relying on the wealthiest and highest income households. Plus, the year has started off with more macro vol than many expected. Still to come, a new Fed Chair to add to the unknown, along with important Supreme Court decisions. We recap the oral arguments in the Cook case on page 5. We also suspect the odds of a rate cut in March, or before June, are underpriced. The Economic Comment begins on page 3. The Week Ahead: Fed ahead We preview the January FOMC meeting on page 8. We expect the Committee to leave policy unchanged and the Chair to offer little forward-looking guidance in the press conference. records.text: 23 January 2026 Fixed Income Blog Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 2 As we have repeatedly noted, it takes a majority of the Committee to set policy, including on the balance sheet. And the Committee has long stated that the fed funds rate is its primary tool to adjust the policy stance – this has been in their consensus strategy statement since 2020 as well as their various balance sheet normalization principles over the past decade. Similarly, there appears to be a consensus on the FOMC to shorten the duration of its Treasury portfolio by moving it towards the universe of Treasuries outstanding. Beyond these considerations, more active use of the balance sheet would run counter to Secretary Bessent’s criticisms of Fed policy. Still, while a meaningful shift in near-term balance sheet policy seems highly unlikely, Rieder might be more inclined than Warsh to use the balance sheet as a tool to respond to future shocks (including market dysfunction), and that should be discounted in curves today. In light of this and the dynami cs observed this week , we think the immediate market reaction to a Rieder nomination could be to flatten the curve. Given the possibility, we are for now taking off the 5y TIPS / 30y nominal UST steepener that we have liked for the last several months (as outlined in the Key Views Table in our US Fixed Income Weekly ), though we it may be appropriate to re -engage the trade down the road. records.text: European Viewpoint | 23 January 2026 7 How has EURDKK coped with the Greenland tensions? There has been renewed focus on the EUR/DKK peg in recent weeks as geopolitical crosscurrents pushed the pair to multi-year highs and in all likelihood triggered a response from the Danish Central Bank. As we discussed in a recent note (FX Watch: Focus on EUR/DKK Peg 20 January 2026) this was only the fourth time since inception that EUR/DKK has traded at these elevated levels. However, we were unequivocal in our view that the central bank would use FX interventions (sell EUR/DKK) to ease the pressure on the de-facto tolerance band. Given ample reserves and an unwavering commitment to EUR/DKK as the primary policy tool, we are confident that the Danes have sufficient FX reserves to withstand further pressure on the peg. Whilst the current period of uncertainty has passed, we cannot say with certainty that this is the end of the debate which likely means limited scope for a trend rally in DKK. More importantly for Danish markets has been the reversal in the forwards market, with 12mth forwards also backing off from their highs. Whilst the EUR/DKK has been front and centre for markets, we think the move in forwards is arguably more important in calibrating market stress. Here, the move has been much more significant, retracing the entire spike since the start of the year. records.text: 2 European Viewpoint | 23 January 2026 Economics: Renewed uncertainty Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) ruben.segura-cayuela@bofa.com Sonali Punhani MLI (UK) sonali.punhani@bofa.com What would be the economic impact of the announced tariffs, if reinstated? The eight countries (Denmark, France, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the UK) which were targeted by the 10% tariff threat account for about 11% of US imports. But it's unclear how the tariffs would be implemented since all but Norway and the UK (2% of imports) are in the EU. Either the tariffs would have to be applied to the entire EU (over 15% of imports), or goods from the other six countries could find their way across the single market to minimise the impact of those tariffs. Unless the tariffs are EU-wide (Trump has not said this so far), we believe the economic impact would be minimal for the region. The more relevant cost would likely come from a persistent spike in uncertainty, the magnitude of which would depend crucially on the size and duration of the shock. As a reminder, for Europe, a persistent one standard deviation jump in trade policy uncertainty (TPU) or economic policy uncertainty can cost up to 80bp of capex within a year. And both trade policy and general economic policy uncertainty are already clearly rising (Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2). It would not put as much production at risk as a Hormuz closure, but it would create a longer-lasting upside of our base case (we assume any Hormuz closure to be relatively quickly mitigated, likely by US naval intervention). Considering that both markets will likely lengthen through 2026, we anticipate the structural upside to remain limited to USD10/bbl for oil and EUR5/MWh for gas. Significant, long-lasting oil and gas price upside in a power vacuum: While scuppered flows through the Strait of Hormuz have the highest price upside, we also believe such an escalation is unlikely and would be relatively short lived. Our base case assumes recent dynamics persist prompting periodic, moderate price spikes. We also assume some form of US intervention is likely, but falls short of regime change, limiting structural price upside. We think such an intervention would create temporary price upside for both oil and gas over our base case (like it did previously), which we otherwise keep unchanged. In the event the Iranian leadership does fall, we would expect a potentially lengthy and challenging power vacuum. In this scenario, military intervention – and the Iranian reaction – would likely create a strong price peak which eventually recedes to structural upsides of USD10/bbl and EUR5/MWh over our base case once the focus shifts to internal political tensions. 23/01/2026 Power vacuum in Iran could create long-term supply disruptions

records.text: M Idea 2 Market Recap Rates bear steepened in a short week in the US as geopolitical tensions eased amid a combination of slightly more muted tariff rhetoric post-Davos and elevated volatility in Japanese markets. From Friday to Tuesday, 30yr JGB yields sold off almost 40bp before rallying back about 25bp as headlines around Prime Minister Takaichi's proposed consumption tax cuts were somewhat balanced by talks of coordination from Finance Minister Katayama to restore confidence along with the January MPM. While much of the focus in the US was shifted to events happening outside its borders, we would be remiss to not discuss price action here. Domestic risk assets were mixed as the S&P ended the week effectively unchanged, vol was slightly higher, and credit tightened. The IG cash index closed last night at 71bp, the tights since 1998, while HY closed at 250, the tights since 2007. We'll note our credit strategists suggest that the GSE program supports strong technicals in credit for now and that headline spreads are not as tight as previous instances make them look once you adjust for things like the price, duration, and ratings of the index. Mortgages, on the other hand, had less of an exciting week on the top level as the index was unchanged in OAS. Our top-down forecast is primarily driven by the following factors: • We expect stronger nominal GDP growth across APAC, which should translate into higher incremental corporate funding needs and, in turn, support higher net supply. Our Asia economics team forecasts higher nominal GDP growth for both APAC and Asia ex-Japan in 2026 and 2027, suggesting funding needs should remain firm over the next two years. Growth will remain uneven across the region, but the breadth improves: seven APAC economies are expected to post ≥5% y/y nominal GDP growth in 2026, up from five in 2025. • We expect USD funding to become cheaper relative to local-currency funding, as our US economics team anticipates further Fed easing into 2H26 while our Asia economics team sees limited scope for additional rate cuts across Asian central banks. Cheaper USD funding should encourage APAC issuers to tilt issuance toward USD bonds, supporting a turn to positive APAC credit net supply. However, even with USD costs easing, we do not expect USD funding to be as cheap relative to APAC local-currency funding as it has been over most of the past two decades. Possible rate hikes: The third group of EM rates markets comprises those where end-of-cycle trades must factor in a real possibility of rate hikes. So far, only Colombia offers a template for this from 2025, but Brazil in 2024 can also be used as an example. The main defining factor for this group has been sticky inflation, an overheating economy and a loose fiscal environment. Hence, emerging markets with a strong growth picture, positive output gaps and genuine inflation pressures can move into this group even if current policy rates look higher than historical norms in real and nominal terms (and above economists’ terminal-rate forecasts). The Colombia and Brazil examples show outright duration shorts may work well for these curves, but that curves may struggle to steepen. We see Poland and Chile as potential candidates for this group. One set of views seems to argue for building up reserves via increasing securities holdings to accommodate the large seasonal swings in the TGA without relying on standing repo operations (SRP). Another group preferred to limit balance sheet size by relying more on repo and conducting RMPs closer to that seasonal demand. The second of these views suggests that there is some downside risks to the level of Fed T-bill demand post Q1 if they choose a framework in which the Fed runs reserves at a lower level and relies on greater use of its standing repo operations to handle fluctuations in the TGA. This would not only mean fewer reserves in the system, but also a situation where there is a bit more pressure in repo markets when there are large upward swings in the TGA. Bank capital rules likely to come in H1 2026 is likely to see proposals for major regulatory changes as well. Adjustments to the eSLR should start to take effect in Q1 as banks can opt in to use the reduced requirements early, with final adoption in Q2. As noted above, we think this will create additional funding market capacity keeping funding pressures at bay along with the other factors noted. The GSE program is likely to focus on conventionals at first, exacerbating roll and price response. Supply is coming in Ginnies, not conventionals. It's likely easier to implement a MIP cut than LLPA change. The move in JGBs has perhaps made life insurance companies find JGBs more attractive than Ginnies. Of course, how much is in the price? We think at this point much of the negative news is already priced in. Were the GSEs to start buying Ginnies, the supply/demand mismatch specifically in Ginnies would become much better. records.text: 8 European Viewpoint | 23 January 2026 Rates: historical comparisons Sphia Salim MLI (UK) Ronald Man MLI (UK) What has been the typical reaction to tariff announcements in EUR rates? Looking at past episodes of tariff announcements by President Trump in 2025, we find that they are typically followed by a rally in front-end EUR rates, including a decline in inflation forwards (1y1y). This is consistent with how our economists present the macro and monetary policy implications of tariffs for the Euro Area: mostly a demand shock that weighs on growth and on the medium term inflation outlook, as opposed to one that creates inflationary concerns. On average, 1y1y €str forwards rallied 5bp over the five business days that followed a tariff announcement impacting the EU (Exhibit 1). However, this average is skewed lower by the rates selloff recorded at the June ECB meeting, days after the last tariff announcement on steel and aluminium. Schatz spreads and 10y BTP-Bund spreads tended to widen, consistent with their typical risk-off behaviour. However, moves in 3m implied rates vol and the 1y cross currency basis have been mixed. While a shock can be thought to drive rates vol higher, this was often offset by the directionality of vol to rates (declining on expectation of lower rates). An outlook of growing availability of USD liquidity vs EUR, coupled with the depreciation pressures on USD around tariff announcements has also led to little systematic widening in cross currency bases

If strong wage growth is confirmed, the certainty of a virtuous cycle from wages to prices will further increase. Furthermore, in April, the projection period of the Outlook Report will shift from the current fiscal 2025-27 to fiscal 2026-28. We anticipate that this will indicate the stable achievement of the 2% price target at an earlier stage of the projection period, thereby providing a basis for justifying a rate hike path towards 1%, the lower bound of the nominal neutral interest rate. Regarding the specific pace of rate hikes, after implementing a 0.25% hike in April (policy interest rate at 1.0%), we expect an additional hike in October, bringing the policy interest rate to 1.25%. Depending on the results of the shunto and the progression of the yen's depreciation, a faster pace of rate hikes could be possible. Subsequent rate hikes will likely depend on developments in the global economy, particularly the U.S. economy. If the Federal Reserve (Fed) were to re-enter a rate hike cycle earlier than anticipated, the BoJ would likely follow suit with further hikes, also from the perspective of addressing upward pressure on import prices due to a weaker yen. And even if the CRA were to secure the most seats, whether this would lead to a change of government would depend on post-election coalition negotiations. In any case, the election outlook appears highly uncertain. With respect to the BoJ’s monetary policy stance, major changes are unlikely even after the election. Still, depending on the election outcome and the FX environment, some subtle adjustments may occur. In scenarios where the LDP secures a single-party majority or the status quo remains intact under a Takaichi administration - and where the JPY is stable or appreciating - we would expect somewhat stronger political pressure on the BoJ to keep rates on hold. However, if the JPY weakens, the administration would likely continue its current stance of reluctantly tolerating rate hikes aimed at addressing the JPY weakness. If the ruling coalition clearly loses its majority and the CRA significantly increases its presence, on the other hand, it may become uncertain which party will form the government. That said, because the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP), which is at the core of the CRA, is relatively supportive of interest rate normalization, policy would likely move somewhat more in the direction of giving the BoJ greater autonomy than at present. However, NOK saw a big rally in recent days. Some of this may have been attributed to concerns around rotations away from Treasuries, though it could also have corresponded with the surge in TTF gas (which has driven Norway’s terms of trade sharply higher; Figure 3). Still, even with the gas rally, NOK appreciation has now taken it to over 1% overvalued against the USD based on fair value, which incorporates both relative rates and relative terms of trade. Additionally, the gas spike has been driven by weather and concerns Europe could run out of gas. However, Citi Commodities sees a low probability that Europe would run out of gas storage before winter ends, and they believe the latest surge of near-term TTF futures is to be faded. The combination of the rotation narrative in Norway being dismissed and a decline in gas prices could present headwinds to the NOK rally and lead to a quick reversal. records.text: Taken together, our results suggest that the ECB usually started moving policy after sizeable inflections in the growth and inflation data which led the staff to make corresponding changes to their projections. The historical record therefore broadly matches the prescription of standard Taylor rules but looks somewhat more responsive than an optimal policy (with the benefit of perfect foresight) would suggest. Looking ahead, the Governing Council is likely to be attentive to the origin, magnitude, and persistence of any deviations of inflation from target. We would, for instance, expect the Council to overlook a small or short-lived deviation owing to a supply shock, unless the spot data inflects noticeably for successive quarters and the staff shifts to projecting a lasting deviation of inflation from target. Our analysis thus supports our expectation that the ECB will remain on hold this year, unless the economic outlook deteriorates materially. The negative impact could extend to the longer expiries, likely causing them to cheapen towards the shorter expiries and flatten the vol term structure. Because the GSEs would likely fund the MBS purchases by issuing mostly short- term debt, many market participants compare it to the Fed’s 2011 Operation Twist. Looking back at how the swaption surface reshaped around Operation Twist, we see that long expiries underperformed with the 5y10y vs 1y10y vol slope flattening over the initial months (Figure 8). Another key takeaway is that Operation Twist’s suppression of vol was more focused on the 10y tails and not the 30y. Implied vols on 30y tails had clearly outperformed 10y tails in a sustained fashion with the 30y vs 10y vol ratio well exceeding 1 (Figure 9). Given that the duration of the MBS is closer to the belly rates rather than the 30y, we see room for 30y tails and right- side vol to outperform 10y tails if the GSEs buy MBS in a more aggressive manner. We still believe short-dated and realized volatility are now too low, given the overall level of macro uncertainty. The core output of the model, the factor, is a latent (unobserved) time series that represents this common economic signal and can be thought of as a weighted average of what many indicators agree on, with the weights learned from historical co-movement. This feature explains why DFMs are particularly well suited for nowcasting. When new data are released, the model effectively asks whether the information confirms or contradicts the existing common signal. In practice, we combine a broad set of timely monthly indicators and link the resulting factors to quarterly GDP growth. Our model uses 17 indicators, spanning PMIs (composite, employment, services, and manufacturing), European Commission business surveys (employment, industry, and construction), as well as expectations for the French Insee industry surveys. These indicators were pre-selected through a procedure designed to identify variables that are most relevant for nowcasting GDP growth. After pre- selection, the DFM always operates on the same set of indicators; it does not further select variables, but continuously re-weights them by extracting a small number of common factors that summarize their shared signal. records.text: The runway for continued equity market broadening The word of the year so far for equity investors is “broadening.” Building on momentum that began in late 2025, SMID-cap US equities and non-US markets have generally outperformed the headline US equity indices in the first few weeks of 2026. The top-heavy S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have each returned 1% YTD. But within the S&P 500, 68% of constituents have generated positive returns, and our preferred measure of market breadth has continued to rebound from its October low (Exhibit 2). Outside of the S&P 500, the Russell 2000 has returned 10%, outperforming the S&P 500 on each of the first 14 trading days of this year. From a fundamental perspective, the improvement in market breadth can be explained by a broadening in the set of opportunities facing investors. The drivers of that opportunity set, including an improving economic growth outlook and friendly Fed policy, have coincided with incremental uncertainty surrounding the earnings outlooks for some of the largest US tech stocks. From a flows perspective, the broadening also reflects a continued shift toward diversification in investor portfolios. A change in allocations with modest implications for the S&P 500 can have large implications for smaller indices. For instance, a rotation of 1% of S&P 500 market cap to the Russell 2000 would represent 19% of market cap for the small-cap index. However, given Iran’s size, diversity, and the lack of coherence between key factions, we believe a power vacuum is the more likely result. And this could in our view be significantly negative for oil and gas production. Seeking regime change through military intervention also implies a higher risk of a relatively strong retaliation. That would put regional facilities at risk, shut in Israeli gas production, and cut off Iranian gas exports to Türkiye. The first two impacts would likely dissipate upon regime change when a power vacuum focuses attention on the domestic political aftermath. Meanwhile, in a regime change scenario without explicit external intervention, we see less potential for upside to materialize. records.text: Historically, when corporate bond spreads reach very tight levels this portends poor excess returns to Treasuries on a go-forward basis as the asymmetry of potential outcomes skews towards widening. Exhibit 2 puts this in context showing the mean and median 12-month forward excess return for months where IG and HY spreads averaged at or below 88bp or 295bp (below the 10th historical percentile), respectively. The obvious takeaway is that both the average and median 12-month excess returns are typically negative when spreads start at these levels. This high level exercise masks some nuance under the surface. We can separate out the prior instances of sub-10th percentile spreads into four primary episodes: 2004/05, early-2007, late-2021, and late-2024. The 2007 and 2021 episodes, which resulted in a credit-driven recession and a very sharp monetary tightening, both led to deeply negative excess returns. The 2004 and 2024 episodes, which resembled the current environment of above-trend real GDP growth and decent yield support much more closely, both led to still-positive excess returns (again, Exhibit 2). Last year provides an instructive example: USD IG and HY indices managed to deliver positive excess returns of 1.2% and 2.6%, respectively, despite beginning the year with spreads of 80bp and 287bp, well inside the 10th historical percentile. There will be another test of this in the next couple of weeks with the pre-election JGB auctions mentioned above, noting that a 20yr JGB auction contributed to Tuesday’s VaR shock. Supply days vs non-supply days: We take a simple approach of comparing daily yield changes on supply days vs non-supply days, inspired by our US Rates Strategy colleagues (see Figure 14, US Rates Weekly: 2026 Outlook – Battle for Accommodation). A UK case study: We begin with a long-term history for the UK, defining supply days as any day with a gilt or linker operation (be it auction, syndication, tender), regardless of its size. Figure 3 looks at the cumulative contribution made to the annual yield change on supply days vs non-supply days. For 2020-23, supply days tended to see lower yields, perhaps helped by QE for much of this period. Moreover, other drivers – namely the hiking cycle – dominated the larger yield moves which were concentrated on non-supply days. For 2024 and 2025, however, supply days tended to push yields higher. records.text: 3 Insights SPOTLIGHT CHARTS Remarkable resilience In line with the theme of this week’s document, real money investor sentiment continues to look through geo-\political concerns. The latest BRS sentiment reading is a solid +6 , marking the 28 th consecutive positive daily reading. Indeed, until a short-lived dip into negative territory in early December, the BRS had enjoyed 140 days of positive daily readings, the longest such run since 2014 and, the third longest since the GFC. That 140 day run commenced a little over a month after Liberation Day as once ag ain a geo -political shock failed to rile markets for anything but the very short-term. Where’s the vol? In line with the sanguine message from real money investors, market pricing is similarly benign. The JP Morgan FX vol index has trended consistently lower since Liberation Day and recently hit its lowest level since March 2024. The VIX index, meanwhile, has been generally trading near 20 or below since early December. The sharp tightening in the Agency MBS basis to start the year has prompted investors to revisit relative value across high-quality spread products, particularly USD IG. In principle, the rebalancing channel is meaningful: nearly $2 trillion sits in actively managed strategies benchmarked to the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index with at least 20% exposure to corporate bonds, so even modest allocation shifts could translate into material flows. The closest analogue is late 2012, when QE3-related basis tightening coincided with MBS underperformance vs. both corporate credit and Treasuries. Holdings data for select large total-return funds suggest managers trimmed MBS and added corporate bonds and Treasuries as current-coupon OAS approached then-record tights (Exhibit 6). Today, those same funds appear modestly underweight corporate credit relative to MBS (again, Exhibit 6), but we think the 2012 playbook has limits. IG valuations are less forgiving at today’s historic tights, and the gap in market depth between agency MBS and corporate bonds should mechanically slow any rotation (Exhibit 7). Netting this out, we expect tighter MBS basis to translate into incremental demand for USD IG at the margin, part of which has likely accrued as IG has tightened 6bp since the January 8th announcement. records.text: in the UK, we stick to our BoE call of cuts in March and June, with risks of less and/or later. Data was clear enough to seal a hold in February, we think. Headline inflation is the obvious candidate for that this week (paired with GDP data last week). But it was a little too mixed to delay a March cut – underlying services inflation and weekly earnings growth continued to moderate, for instance, and payrolls were weak. And January inflation is likely to drop close to 3%. Absent other surprises, that should be enough to trigger the easing bias the BoE still has; hence we keep our call unchanged. Nordic central banks: boring January We expect the Riksbank to keep rates unchanged at 1.75% in January, with broadly unchanged guidance. The recent dataflow is unlikely to alter the policy stance much. We still view risks for the forward rate path as broadly balanced: the likelihood of further cuts has reduced, but rate hikes remain unlikely too. Even a stronger recovery would be unlikely to trigger early hikes, as the economy is far from any “overheating”. A period of sustained growth with slightly accommodative rates is likely needed to (1) absorb slack and (2) anchor inflation at target. We maintain a flat rate path and see any potential hikes as a risk skewed toward 2027 rather than the year ahead. The European Council meeting concluded this week with a sense of relief, as the immediate threat of new US tariffs was averted (and no decision on retaliation). However, this relief was coupled with a growing realisation that the EU must adapt to a rapidly changing geopolitical environment. The recent threats to Greenland's sovereignty have brought this into sharp focus, serving as further evidence of an unraveling post-1945 international order. These events highlight the EU's strategic vulnerabilities, including its dependencies on the US for defence, Russia for energy, and global trade for growth, reinforcing the need for the bloc to build its own economic and political power to protect its interests. In response to this shifting landscape, there is a building consensus that the EU must pursue greater "strategic autonomy." Key policy discussions are now centered on increasing defence spending towards the new 3.5% NATO target, accelerating the competitiveness agenda laid out in the Draghi report, and deepening the Single Market to unlock internal growth potential. Furthermore, policymakers are exploring avenues for common funding for "European public goods" like defence, and the European Commission has tasked the Cypriot EU Presidency with developing a new European security strategy. On a separate note, all the geopolitical developments of the past month and especially the latest on Greenland emphasize the importance of defence spending as well as defence capabilities, with France well positioned to benefit from a “geopolitical premium” (sole independent nuclear power in the EU) as we flagged in our last year’s publication In Defense of OAT . Stronger EU cohesion and solidarity should also benefit OATs at this juncture, especially when France is under an EDP with a risk of overshooting its deficit target. Finally, it’s worth repeating a comment made last year, that the tightening in 10y OAT/Bund is disguising the relative cheapness of OATs vs other EGB spreads. 10y OAT/Bund is currently at the tighter end of its past 6 months range but when we look at the spread of OAT vs the average of all othe r EGBs (excl. Germany), this spread has stayed stubbornly high since last August. In summary, OATs could benefit near-term from: i) unique defence capabilities of France, ii) stronger EU cohesion & solidarity (potentially translating to more leniency with respect to EDP & deficit targets), iii) reduction in political risk premia should elections be avoided, iv) current cheap valuations. In the United States, oil production has also been affected by ~250 kbd due to winter weather, though the impact so far remains relatively modest We estimate that US crude and condensate production in January 2026 will decline by around 250 kbd relative to December. This is similar to the 297 kbd lost in January 2025, but significantly less than the 780 kbd lost in January 2024 (Figure 15). Cold weather is expected to affect a large part of the country, with the most acute impact concentrated over the weekend period, while freezing temperatures are forecast to extend from Texas and New Mexico all the way east toward Georgia and north into New York. Initial news reports already point to production losses in the Bakken and Oklahoma’s Anadarko Basin. However, as freezing conditions are expected to be intermittent rather than prolonged, the exact extent of disruptions remains difficult to quantify in real time. On debt supply, our economists view the overall baseline debt-to-GDP trajectory as relatively benign, but PM Takaichi’s call for a snap election nonetheless raises the near-term uncertainty around the fiscal path amid a shifting political landscape. Even if the baseline expectation for the r-g arithmetic is favorable, evidence from other markets (e.g., the US and UK) underscores how front-end rate selloffs can interact with the repricing in fiscal risk premia in non-linear ways. This can lead to bouts of long-end repricing that create a level of persistence in bond risk premia long after the initial shock, with the long shadow of the 2022 Gilt crisis setting a clear example. This outcome is not embedded in our base case for Japan, where we expect 10s30s to end the year at 120bp, still somewhat above 2024 levels but firmly flatter than the peak of 2H2025 steepness. This procedure allows the budget law to be enacted without a parliamentary vote, unless MPs bring forward a motion of no confidence and a majority supports it, an outcome that would bring down both the bill and the government. In practice, article 49.3 will be used three times: for the income part, the spending part, and for the whole budget, meaning various motions of no confidence are likely to be triggered through this process. However, the bar to get a majority on the confidence vote is high, as the government made further concessions to the centre-left Socialist Party, and as a result, they argued they would not vote in favor of any coming motion of no confidence. Last month, we contributed to a Citi Economics publication that examined the US fiscal picture, with a number of key insights from our asset class specialists (The Still-Rising US Public Debt: Twelve Questions & Answers). The takeaway was that fiscal health is a lingering concern worth monitoring, but not an immediate issue for equity markets. Yet, the ’22 gilts episode was noted as a reminder that there is a point at which a lingering concern can turn to an immediate issue given a catalyst. Another Warning Shot This week, we saw another warning sign in Japan with bond markets pushing back against proposed pro-cyclical fiscal stimulus measures. As our rates strategy colleagues noted (see Japan Rates – BoJ/MoF may not step in), proposed tax cuts alongside above-target inflation were ill-received by JGB investors. The larger concern for us is if this is a signal for how US rates could react to similar upcoming fiscal catalysts ahead of the midterms. Our takeaway is that this risk factor should be considered but should not drive US equity allocation decisions for the year ahead. Volatility Event Ahead? Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: US Equity Strategy 23 January 2026 Citi Research 2 We have described our ’26 outlook as a “persistent but volatile bull” (2026 Outlook: A Persistent But Volatile Bull). The issue, of course, is that while it is easy to say “expect volatility, ” it is often very difficult to more precisely anticipate such events other than to bucket them as tail risks. Similarly, we often note that the biggest risk to US equities is often “shock effects. ” Yet, shock effects, by definition, entail macro or political forces that are hard to predict. Thus, we are constantly surveilling the landscape for potential disruptions that could potentially trigger a volatility event. One such risk is a more meaningful backup in 10yr yields. Equity markets have mostly taken the rate backup from a late October low of 3.94% to the recent 4.25% level in stride. Earlier this week, pushback from Japanese bond markets surfaced at the prospects of funding proposed fiscal stimulus. Given the ongoing push for additional fiscal stimulus measures ahead of the US midterms, equity investors should have a frame of reference for the risk that another bond vigilante episode could bring about. T o be clear, this does not change our constructive ’26 outlook storyline, but it does show some characteristics of shorter-term volatility event risk. The chair could note that they will be closely watching how financial markets continue to evolve as they gauge the potential impact of these events on the economic outlook. With respect to economic fundamentals, although Powell will likely continue to emphasize that downside risks remain prominent for the labor market, his tone may sound somewhat more sanguine. The case for downside risks remains. Employment gains are still subdued, and the breadth of those gains is still particularly narrow, with only a few sectors (mostly education and health care services) adding labor. In this sense, the low hiring dynamic has not changed and the labor market remains susceptible to shocks. At the same time, there are some reasons to be more optimistic at the margin. First and foremost, growth momentum remains robust. After a strong Q3 (4.3%), real GDP growth looks to have remained firm in Q4, against most expectations for a sharp deceleration. We expect this sturdy growth backdrop to continue, and it appears Fed officials have generally become more optimistic about the growth outlook as well. While the recent increase in long-term rates likely reflects a rise in risk premiums, current long-term rates are not excessively high when viewed against Japan’s inflation, the real economy, and US rate levels, as discussed in our previous report. Having exited the Yield Curve Control (YCC) regime of directly controlling long-term yields, the BoJ is in the process of normalizing policy toward a market-determined rate environment; thus, the threshold for emergency operations appears high. That said, in the interim review scheduled for June, we believe the BoJ is likely—based on JGB market stability considerations—to slow the pace of JGB purchase reductions starting in April 2027. While this is a risk scenario and not our base case, depending on market developments we cannot fully rule out the possibility that the BoJ will slow the pace of reductions immediately after July 2026, or even temporarily pause the reduction in purchase amounts from April 2027 onward.

LLC Global Markets Daily: JGBs in 2026: A Narrow Path to Modest Relief 23 January 2026 | 1:41PM EST JGBs have started 2026 in particularly volatile fashion, with long-dated JGB n forward yields now on par with the US. While substantial JGB underperformance (higher yields) was our baseline for 2025, we think current price action has taken yields too high vs our current economic forecasts and continue to see 10y JGBs at 2.0% at end-2026 vs forwards of 2.60%. That said, the upcoming Japanese election skews the risks towards more n inflationary fiscal policy, which is why we see the near-term risks skewed to higher yields vs our forecast path. Recent policy announcements, including a reduction in long-end supply, should help to address the supply/demand mismatch at the long-end of the curve, but fiscal risk premium will likely remain durable until the macro picture becomes clearer. We think the eventual combination of steady BOJ hikes (with risks skewed n towards acceleration) and a moderation of inflation towards the end of 2026 should cap long-end JGB volatility and flatten the curve vs forwards. The key upside risk to yields comes from stronger-than-expected underlying inflation, which could reignite the risk that the BOJ falls behind the curve, leading to a rebuild in long-end risk premia. records.text: izing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 50k in 2026 after coming in at 15k in 2H25. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate ticking up to just 4.5% in 4Q25, where it should remain in 1H26 before dropping to 4.3% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed cut rates by 25bp to 3.5-3.75% at its December meeting, as expected. The Fed also announced reserve management purchases of $40bn per month, starting December 12. We think the majority of the committee wants to go back on hold. But Powell’s decision will come down to the downside risks in the spot labor data (unemployment rate). Our base case remains that the Fed won't cut again under Powell. We expect only two more 25bp cuts this year in June and July. This leaves our projection of the terminal rate unchanged at 3.0-3.25%.

records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 3 Executive Summary 2026 will be the year where the story of supply - especially US IG issuance - takes center stage to drive equity outperformance relative to fixed income, and government bonds relative to corporate credit. For most of the past few years, the issuance story had taken a back seat as AI and macro narratives dominated. But as AI capex funding needs continue to grow and animal spirits in equity markets revive M&A activity, getting a gauge on relative supply will be important to get a gauge on relative performance, especially when micro and macro fundamentals look solid. We see several themes for global fixed income supply in 2026: AI capex spend: We see AI-related capex as a durable multi-year theme and push back on the idea that we're in a capex bubble that will pop any time. This means ~US$2.9 trillion in data center related capex over the next several years, and roughly half will need to be financed through credit markets. US IG will see the bulk of issuance - we expect US$1trn of net supply this year - but securitized credit markets could also see heavy supply. With some credit segments relatively well-insulated from a supply perspective, expect differentiated performance within spread products, with US IG and Data Center ABS underperfoming. records.text: Europe's economies send mixed signals PMI's show Germany and France diverge In the euro area, the next ECB meeting (5 February) is still a couple of weeks out, but this and next week bring important data for the policymakers. The January flash PMIs were steady at 51.5, slightly below our and consensus expectations. In level terms, this means the PMIs started Q1 0.8pt below their Q4 25 average, indicating that the recent acceleration in economic activity perhaps lost some momentum at the start of the new year. In addition, the PMIs underscored geographic divergence, as the German reading improved while the French fell further below 50. The periphery, which had been the bright spot of euro area PMIs in recent quarters, continued to edge slightly lower. Across sectors, services activity lost further momentum at the start of the year, while manufacturing output firmed, returning to expansion. Next week will include the release of country-level and euro area preliminary Q4 GDP . Both soft and hard data for Q4 point to some upside risks to our 0.2% q/q forecast, with the latest iteration of our nowcast model suggesting growth of about 0.3% q/q. We will also get the January Ifo business survey, the European Commission’s January consumer and business surveys, and the euro area December unemployment rate. records.text: 23 January 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 43 Longer-run perspective on real term premia Global term premia are up sharply today on geopolitical tensions and spillovers from Japan. In the US, the increases have been in real term premia, as the forward breakeven curve is little changed. To gauge where the moves leave things, the chart below looks at a measure of real Treasury term premium, which following our standard approach is calculated as the front-end-hedged slope of the TIPS curve. Relative to the post-2004 period over which TIPS have actively traded, real 10s30s TP today sits at all-time highs (dark blue). But for perspective the chart also includes “backcasts” of this measure to the earlier pre-TIPS period (light blue). To do so, we regress TIPS BEIs on nominal yields, CPI, oil, and the S&P 500 over 2004-present. We then use these coefficient estimates and values of the explanatory variables in the earlier period to construct TIPS yields and, by extension, real TP going back to the late 1970s. The key takeaway from this simple exercise – which admittedly assumes stability in correlations amongst the variables – is that, while real 10s30s TP today sits at a historic post-TIPS high, it does not look nearly as stretched relative to a longer history; it is near late-1990s levels and substantially below levels reached in the 1970s and 1980s. She also pledged to abandon the convention of drafting the initial budget on the assumption that a supplementary budget would follow, and she noted that the FY2026 initial budget announced in December did not fully reflect this policy as the formulation process had already begun before she became leader of the Liberal Democratic Party. This implies the FY2027 initial budget could be substantially larger than FY2026’s; her statement also leaves room for a sizable supplementary budget in FY2026, in our view. Because Japan is already operating near full employment, any further expansionary fiscal policy would add to inflationary pressure, we believe. All else equal, the BoJ would need to revise its inflation forecasts and its risk assessment, which should prompt it to consider accelerating the pace of rate hikes. We expect cuts in March/June This, along with a looser labour market and cooling in pay, keeps the door open for further cuts. We expect cuts in March and June to 3.25%. Having said that, the BoE is turning more cautious as it reaches neutral. Key would be wage settlements for 2026 (out in February MPR) and wage expectations, which, if they stay elevated and along with the BoE’s caution, can increase risks of a delay to April and pose upside risks to terminal. Details: Food, tobacco and airfares drove the rise The jump in December inflation was driven by food, tobacco and airfares. Tobacco duty was increased on 26 November 2025, whereas in 2024 it was increased on 30 October, causing a pickup in alcohol and tobacco inflation from 4.0% to 5.2%. Food inflation rose from 4.2% to 4.5% but below the BoE’s expectation of 5.3%. Services inflation rose from 4.4% to 4.5% driven by a rise in airfares inflation and accommodation. Air fares rose by 28.6%m/m in December 2025 vs. 16.2% last year (which were fairly weak due to flight return days on Christmas Eve). The UK is walking a tightrope – it wants to preserve its economic and strategic relationship with the US while standing united with the EU on its position on Greenland. Moreover, the risks of higher inflation and growth implications from a potential trade war are also likely to reduce the UK’s overall appetite to retaliate. Having said that, last year, the UK compiled a list of US products that could be the target of tariffs. The list covers 27% of UK imports from the US but avoids goods that are critical to UK supply chains. Although these tariffs were never implemented after the negotiation of the US-UK trade deal, they could be used if the Greenland situation and the trade war escalate again. Unlike the EU, the UK doesn’t have an Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI), meaning it lacks a formal instrument to retaliate via services. In line with this, it also raised its GDP growth forecasts for FY25-FY26 and its BoJ core inflation forecasts (ex. fresh food and energy) for FY25-FY27 (Exhibit 1). Elsewhere, it made no major revisions to its future risk factors or risk balance, merely adding language citing the potential for exchange rate developments to affect underlying CPI inflation through changes in inflation expectations. Overall, we think these changes signal the BoJ's growing confidence in achieving its price stability target alongside its growing concerns about recent JPY weakness, in line with its comments at the December MPM. Press conference: Little new news BoJ Governor Ueda’s remarks at the post-MPM press conference offered very little new information on the outlook for rate hikes or potential bond buying operations. This is the single most consequential theme for 2026, yet visibility remains limited. The election is still distant, making definitive assessments premature. Thus far, 2026 has begun much as 2025 ended: an expectation of a polarized race; lingering uncertainty over the viability of a Flávio Bolsonaro candidacy; growing pressure on Tarcísio de Freitas to enter the race; and continued fragmentation on the right. Meanwhile, the incumbent, President Lula, is highly likely to seek re election. On the left, Lula has effectively consolidated the field as the sole standard bearer. Guilherme Boulos’ move into Lula’s cabinet reinforced the president’s dominance over the left leaning electorate and removed a potential alternative candidacy. While Lula’s age remains a non trivial consideration—he would be 81 in 2027 and 85 by the end of a new term in 2030—there is currently no indication that health concerns would prevent him from running. records.text: David Mericle +1(212)357-2619 | david.mericle@gs.com Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC US Daily: January FOMC Preview: Further to Go, but Not for a While 24 January 2026 | 8:22PM EST The January FOMC meeting is likely to be uneventful, with no change to the fed n funds rate, only minor changes to the statement, and few hints about the future policy path. Chair Powell is likely to emphasize that the FOMC has just delivered three cuts that should help to stabilize the labor market and is well positioned for now while it assesses their impact. If the labor market does stabilize this year, as we and the FOMC expect, further n rate cuts would be less urgent. While 15 of 19 FOMC participants anticipate that some additional cuts will be appropriate eventually, the leadership will likely want less urgent normalization cuts to be backed by a stronger consensus than the last cut in December was. This will require more convincing progress on inflation. Participants will have different ways of assessing that progress, but it will likely take time for the data to be clear enough to persuade some of them. As a result, we have penciled in the next 25bp rate cut in June, followed by a final n cut in September to 3-3.25%. records.text: central part of the case brought by Governor Cook’s attorney today — that notice and a hearing is a requirement here and that Governor Cook was granted neither. Justice Kagan repeatedly asked the question of whether a hearing was required and Justice Gorsuch questioned what such a hearing would look like. Sauer argued that the Federal Reserve Act does not require notice, or a hearing: "It's not stated explicitly in the statute. And Congress knows how to provide that." Sauer also stated that Governor Cook already has been given adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. On the question of adequate notice, Justice Jackson questioned whether Cook's attorney thought a social media post was sufficient notice: " are you conceding that a posting on social media is sufficient notice in a situation like this when the President is seeking to remove a governor for — for cause? records.text: Sven Jari Stehn +44(20)7774-8061 | jari.stehn@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Alexandre Stott +33(1)4212-1108 | alexandre.stott@gs.com Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE - Paris Branch European Daily: ECB—The Hurdle for Action 22 January 2026 | 6:13PM GMT With the ECB widely expected to remain on hold this year, we explore the hurdle n for monetary policy changes using a range of approaches. First, we document that year-over-year growth and inflation usually decline by 0.4pp in the four quarters ahead of rate cuts, and vice versa. The staff projections for growth and inflation typically change by 0.5pp and 0.2pp, respectively, ahead of policy shifts. Second, we use a simple Taylor rule to gauge the hurdle for policy action. This n exercise would imply a 25bp move in response to a deviation of around 0.5pp for growth or inflation. But the ECB usually cuts at least twice and by more than 50bp when away from the lower bound. The hurdle to move policy by at least 50bp under a Taylor rule would therefore be twice as large and broadly matches the ECB’s historical record. Third, simulations with our small macro model of the Euro area suggest that the n policy response would increase with the magnitude and persistence of the inflation deviation. We find that an optimal policy would only respond by moving by at least 50bp if a one-year inflation deviation is at least 0.6pp or if a 0.2pp deviation is sustained for more than two years. Former allies: The LDP and Komeito had been cooperating very closely in elections. LDP candidates in single-member districts asked their supporters to vote for Komeito in the proportional block and Komeito supporters were asked to back LDP candidates in the districts. Although Komeito formally left the coalition in October last year, we think the LDP may well have assumed that personal ties and local arrangements meant it could still expect some level of cooperation in many constituencies. The CDP–Komeito merger, however, is likely to upend that cooperation; a significant portion of Komeito’s organizational vote could now flow to CDP candidates. Komeito’s vote total is generally estimated at about 20,000 per constituency, and assuming a 50% turnout, total votes cast per district are roughly 150,000–160,000 on average. And so, even if only part of the 20,000 Komeito votes transfer to the new CRA party, the impact may be significant. In the October 2024 lower-house election, LDP candidates beat CDP opponents by less than 10,000 votes in 20 districts. Regaining votes: While the LDP currently benefits from Takaichi’s high personal approval, support for the party itself remains below 40% in most polls – similar to that seen in the slump that preceded the LDP’s heavy losses in the 2024 election. BoJ review: JPY vigilance sends hawkish signal The BoJ wrapped up its 22-23 December monetary policy meeting (MPM) with policy rates unchanged at 0.75%, as widely expected. The decision was reached by an 8-1 vote with Policy Board member Takata dissenting in favor of a hike to 1.0% (he "considered that the price stability target had been more or less achieved and that, with overseas economies being in a recovery phase, risks to prices in Japan were skewed to the upside"). The BoJ also maintained its guidance stating that it will "continue to raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation [...] in accordance with improvement in economic activity and prices [...] given that real interest rates are at significantly low levels” ( Figure 4, Figure 5). However, on the move up, both gas and power curves in Europe have flattened significantly, with moves in the front-month contract propagating along longer-dated tenors. This has resulted in a curve that lacks seasonality and looks too expensive from H2 2026 and beyond, in our view, and we expect power prices come off on lower gas prices combined with increased renewable generation. In particular, we see downside to Q3 and Q4 prices, mainly because incoming LNG supply should depress gas prices towards the end of the year. We expect lower gas prices and renewable capacity buildout to weigh on 2027 prices, with German and French power prices to average EUR77/MWh and EUR53/MWh, respectively. Carbon relevance rises for European power prices: The correlation between power and carbon prices strengthened last year, with upside to EUA prices supporting power prices, particularly in Germany due to reliance on coal and lignite generation. Meanwhile, gas has taken a back seat as bearishness on incoming supply saw prices diverge from the rest of the European energy complex. records.text: US Economics Weekly23 January 2026 ab 21 Philadelphia nonmanufacturing improves but still weak The FRB of Philadelphia nonmanufacturing activity index rose 17.4 points to -4.2 in January, a level unseen since October 2024 but still in contraction. The new orders index rose 5.3 points to 5.5, the sales or revenues index rose 12.7 points to 24.8, and unfilled orders fell -5.4 points to 2.1. Firms in the third district reported a modest increase in full- time employment and sharp drop in part-time employment. The index for the number of full-time employees rose 2.2 points to 9.7, the part-time component fell 15.3 points to 0.4. Prices paid remain elevated while prices received returned near its 2015-2019 average of 14.2. The prices paid index fell 2.4 points to 34.5, and the prices received component fell 3.0 points to 13.2. Expectations for growth were more widespread and the six-month outlook rose 29.4 points to 10.3. Special questions from the Philadelphia survey were collected from January 5 to January 12 and compared cost adjustments from 2025 to cost expectations for 2026, see here. Among the categories, the average actual wage increase was 2.8% in 2025 and expectations were for an average increase of 3.0% in 2026. Inflation in other input costs was expected to moderate on average. The decree reflects the idea of repatriating a large chunk of Colombia’s overseas assets, and cites the potential boost to infrastructure and other productive sectors as a key motivation. How likely is the decree to be implemented? This will be highly dependent on the outcome of the May presidential election, in our view. records.text: M Global Foundation 8 Supply Outlook DM government bonds Across the G7, we expect net bond supply should amount to US$2.56 trillion in 2026, down 11% Y/Y, after central bank purchases, of which we expect none. Uncertainty over the future of fiscal policy across the G7 should keep investor expectations malleable and subject government bond markets to supply-related gyrations. We expect gross government bond supply (not including bills) to increase by US$76 billion in 2026 versus 2025 – representing a 10% Y/Y increase. After netting out redemptions, bond net issuance across the G7 should actually decrease by US$317 billion – amounting to a 11% Y/Y decrease. Net issuance decreases in the US, the euro area, Japan, and New Zealand. How should investors think about supply and its impact on price? Sovereign supply moves markets the most when expectations change for the sovereign supply outlook (see Between a Rock and a Hard Place, April 17, 2020). In 2026, surprises to the outlook for fiscal policy seem most likely to change expectations for the sovereign supply outlook. This means that bond yields can fall (rise) if investors come to expect less (more) supply than they thought before – even if that supply is more (less) than what they had to buy previously. For more, see our 2026 Global Macro Strategy Outlook, November 23, 2025. records.text: ECB—The Hurdle for Action The Governing Council has emphasised that ECB policy is in a “good place” given resilient growth, target-consistent inflation dynamics and a broadly neutral level of interest rates. But President Lagarde has also noted that the current level of rates is not in a “fixed place” and that the Governing Council will respond to changes in the outlook to maintain medium-term price stability. Chief economist Lane, for example, has argued that monetary policy should (i) overlook small deviations of inflation from target, (ii) always respond to large and persistent deviations, and (iii) tailor the response of policy to the origin of moderate deviations. We therefore explore the hurdle for policy action with a range of approaches. Gauging Thresholds for Policy Adjustment First, we document how the economic outlook typically evolved in the run-up to historical policy shifts. To do so, we look at the start of all cutting and hiking cycles since 1999 (Exhibit 1). This gives us 11 total episodes with 8 cut episodes and 3 periods with hikes. All but one of these episodes (in 2019) involved at least two cuts, with a cumulative change in the policy rate of at least 50bp, except at the lower bound (in 2014, 2015 and 2019). Given the small number of observations, we pool the episodes together, focus on the onset of cuts and flip the sign of the episodes with hikes to create a larger sample. records.text: s largely eclipsed in Davos by the intense geopolitical noise was the threat from rising public debt. Sure, Japan's bond sell-off was noted and Trump's turnaround on Greenland was largely ascribed to the pressure on US Treasury yields after the president's earlier escalation. But the underlying issue of G7 economies' inability or unwillingness to rein in fiscal deficit dynamics that look increasingly unsustainable was left aside amid the headline- grabbing geopolitical drama. This negligence could backfire at some point, as this week's developments in Japan highlighted. Tax cut plans spark a sell-off in Japan Markets reacted sharply to PM Takaichi's campaign pledge to suspend for two years the sales tax on food and beverages, costing ¥5 trillion ($31.6 billion) per year. This is not a particularly large amount, but a few things likely shocked markets. First, this is a sharp shift for Takaichi, and it means all parties now advocate some form of a food sales tax cut. Second, while Takaichi said the cut would not be deficit-financed, there is no credible, detailed alternative plan. Finally, temporary tax cuts have a way of becoming permanent, and the government would struggle to reverse it in 2028, an upper house election year. The result was that JGB yields spiked this week, with the 40-year point exceeding 4%. The sell-off eased later in the week, but yields remain much higher. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 5 Executive Summary 2026 will be the year where the story of supply - especially US IG issuance - takes center stage to drive equity outperformance relative to fixed income, and government bonds relative to corporate credit. For most of the past few years, the issuance story had taken a back seat as AI and macro narratives dominated. But as AI capex funding needs continue to grow and animal spirits in equity markets revive M&A activity, getting a gauge on relative supply will be important to get a gauge on relative performance, especially when micro and macro fundamentals look solid. We see several themes for global fixed income supply in 2026: AI capex spend: We see AI-related capex as a durable multi-year theme and push back on the idea that we're in a capex bubble that will pop any time. This means ~US$2.9 trillion in data center related capex over the next several years, and roughly half will need to be financed through credit markets. US IG will see the bulk of issuance - we expect US$1trn of net supply this year - but securitized credit markets could also see heavy supply. With some credit segments relatively well-insulated from a supply perspective, expect differentiated performance within spread products, with US IG and Data Center ABS underperfoming. records.text: 23 January 2026 Japan Monetary Policy Watch Page 2 Deutsche Securities Inc. 1. Policy decision: Status quo maintained, but Takata proposed a rate hike The BoJ decided at today's Monetary Policy Meeting (MPM) to maintain the short- term policy interest rate (the uncollateralized overnight call rate target) at 0.75%, as widely expected. However, in the vote on the proposal, policy board member Takata cast a dissenting vote and submitted a counter-proposal of a rate hike. As noted in our preview memo, Takata has consistently indicated his view that the 2% price stability target has been largely achieved. From this perspective, it is a natural logical conclusion to reduce the degree of monetary accommodation and raise the policy interest rate toward at least 1%, which is estimated to be the lower bound of the nominal neutral interest rate. This rate hike proposal represents putting that idea into action and can be seen as a clear indication of his intention to lead future discussions on rate hikes. In addition to Takata, board member Tamura also dissented from the contents of the Outlook Report. Since Tamura anticipates achieving the price stability target at an earlier timing, it is highly likely that he will propose an interest rate hike in the near future. 2. records.text: 23 January 2026 US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 15 EUR STIR: Terminal rates and tariffs 2026 edition Soniya Sadeesh | Strategist | +44-20-754-73091 Note: This note was originally published on 21 January 2026. Last year we made the observation that tariff announcements were a key driver of market pricing policy rates in the Eurozone materially below neutral. The impact this time around has been far more muted, consistent with the broader market reaction. Terminal rate pricing rallied 3 bp to price around 6bps of cuts this week. Whilst minor, the price action also stood out in relation to the rebound in near term inflation forwards (which again highlights the contrast to dynamics last April). Recent comments from Lagarde have played up the uncertainty rather than the immediate potential tariff impact to inflation. At the same time, one might assume recent events also indicate upside risks to defense spending. On margin, it does suggest that the former has been more relevant this week at least for the immediate policy path. We remain long TKYM6 where the mild basis widening this week also validates the preference for expressing it in €STR. Page 4 While the labor market backdrop may have brightened somewhat, t he inflation picture has become messier since the December FOMC meeting. Fed officials have generally echoed their prior comments around an expectation that a disinflationary trend remains in place. The underpinnings of that story were mostly that shelter inflation should decline over time with the potential to undershoot pre-covid run rates and tariffs will likely manifest as a one -time price level shock that will begin to unwind in the second half of the year. Fundamentally, these stories remain in place. However, the disinflationary path is not as clear-cut as believed just a month ago. The government shutdown is likely to move a portion of measured inflation from 2025 to 2026 due to how the BLS dealt with price data. The skew of data collection towards the second half of Nov ember pushed some inflation into December. The carry forward assumption for some of the regional indices is also likely to push some inflation into January. Finally, the carry forward assumption on shelter will push inflation for primar y rents and OER from October 2025 to April 2026. If these were the only stories, the Fed could likely look through these distortions and continue to emphasize a disinflationary trend. Beyond these considerations there are some reasons to remain cautious about the inflation outlook . We expect December core PCE to print 0.4% month -over- month

Across all Treasury coupon auctions, the share of foreign and international allotments surged to high of 18%, substantially above the average of 11% in the preceding 12 months. Impressively, foreign allotments were robust across the board, except for the 2 -year floater auction (which typically sees weaker foreign allotments compared to nominal and TIPS auctions). December marked the largest allocations to foreign investors sinc e early 2022, just before inflation became a major concern and Treasury yields surged. Today’s chart shows the foreign allotments share against foreign official holdings of long -term Treasuries, reported in the Treasury TIC data. The two series generally line up with each other, possibly because foreign central banks and reserve managers ten d to favor liquid benchmark Treasuries and accumulate them through auctions, whereas foreign private investors transact more frequently in off the off-the-runs in the secondary market. records.text: M Global Foundation 20 Demand Outlook Euro area EGB demand in 2026 should look broadly similar to 2025, with banks, asset managers and foreign investors providing the bulk of support. For many investors the absolute level of yields or spreads is a significant determinant of demand, but ratings can also play a part. The key headwind is ECB QT: roughly €300bn of 2026 EGB maturities are expected not to be reinvested, adding to the amount markets must absorb (with QT slowing slightly in 2027). Euro area banks should be a major anchor through 2026 as yields, swap spreads and deposit growth stay supportive. Foreign demand has been unusually strong across euro area countries, though Japan’s interest remains modest versus past cycles and reserve-manager demand looks stable. Finally, Dutch pension reforms are unlikely to spark meaningful selling; any reductions should be gradual and concentrated in higher-rated sovereigns, with the transition still supportive for bonds versus swaps. We expect US corporate credit demand to stay healthy in 2026. Our forecast for steeper treasury curves historically supports credit demand: lower front-end yields push marginal buyers out the curve and reduce FX-hedging costs for overseas investors. We also think insurance appetite, which was a key anchor in the credit market stays healthy due to long end rates remaining elevated. We also expect EUR corporate credit demand to remain robust. records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 28 November) Real GDP contracted in Q3 for the first negative growth in six quarters, reflecting a sharp drop in housing investment and sluggish exports linked to tariffs. However, as the former was driven by institutional factors, we expect a return to positive growth from Q4. Looking ahead, we expect growth of around 1% on average due primarily to firm capital investment on the back of structural factors such as labor-saving expenditures and stable consumption stemming from a recovery in the real income environment under slowing inflation. Although the economic measures decided by the Takaichi administration are limited in terms of their growth-boosting effect relative to scale, they are likely to provide a certain degree of support to the economy. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. Furthermore, services inflation has become increasingly robust as the dynamic synergy between wages and prices strengthens on the back of irreversible structural changes in the labor market.
