End-of-cycle carry trades: The second group brings together markets where central banks are approaching their terminal rate without an obvious overheating, excessive fiscal spending and/or unanchored inflation expectations. When the next move is unclear (a hike or a cut), the curves need to start building a term premium to justify duration risks. Hence, similar to the experience in CZK and KRW markets, these curves build some steepness starting with the very front end even if a near-term hike looks unlikely. However, once these curves are steep enough, they will also start looking much more attractive in carry and rolldown terms, particularly for long-term investors – especially given the lack of any negative feedback loop coming from a weaker FX. Based on such thinking, we recently raised our estimate for the terminal rate from 1.5% to 2% (see BoJ: Raising our terminal rate forecast to 2%, dated 16 January). Higher prices have eroded households’ real purchasing power, and repeated spending increases and tax cuts designed to offset that erosion have kept personal consumption resilient, which in turn has sustained price pressure. A zero-rating of the food consumption tax would likely temporarily reduce headline CPI by about 1.5pp, but the resulting boost to aggregate demand would push the underlying inflation trend higher. Risk of accelerated hikes: We project the policy-rate trajectory as follows: 1.0% in Q2 2026, 1.25% in Q4 2026, 1.5% in Q2 2027, 1.75% in Q4 2027, and 2.0% in Q2 2028. However, an expansionary fiscal stance could compress the timetable, prompting an earlier move. An acceleration might not stem solely from lower real rates fueling yen depreciation and inflation. Persistent low real rates can become embedded in household and corporate expectations, encouraging more aggressive investment, faster credit growth, and rising real-estate prices. records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy Too much, too soon EUR rates have been caught in geopolitical crosscurrents as a combination of tariff risk and JGB spillovers pivot steepened the curve. Heightened uncertainty should keep rate hike discussion at bay on growth concerns. In EGBs, we discuss the outlook for rating actions in H1. Slow down please, the year has just begun. The US administration has kept the geopolitical news tape whirring at warp speed since the turn of the year with the latest headlines around Greenland and tariffs setting alarm bells in Europe. To add to this turbulence and discussions around a potential return of the 'Sell America' trade , the volatility in long-end JGBs has also reverberated across global fixed income. On back of this tariff versus fiscal tango, curves pivot steepened with EUR2s30s c. 10bp steeper before flattening back as President Trump dropped his tariff threat on European nations following a framework deal being reached on Greenland. Amidst the crosscurrents that EUR rates found themselves in this week, the growth, inflation and monetary policy implications of renewed tariff risks for the EUR curve was in particular focus. As our economists discuss in Tariffs 3.0, Greenland-related developments pose more downside risks to the euro area and UK growth outlook, and will likely have a disinflationary impulse when taking into account all potential channels through which they would operate. records.text: Japan Macro Watch | 23 January 2026 3 Rates: No clear message to support the JGB market As broadly expected, the BoJ kept its monetary policy unchanged at the January MPM. The BoJ did not send any signals or outline potential triggers for conducting ad‑hoc bond‑buying operations or funds‑supplying operations against pooled collateral to provide support to the bond market. Following the release of the statement and the Outlook Report, JGB futures fell by roughly 0.3 yen, reflecting the upward revision to the BoJ’s median inflation outlook (all items less fresh food and energy) and suggesting that some market participants had expected the BoJ to signal bond‑supportive operations. The market‑implied BoJ policy rate for the April MPM is now around 0.9%. It rose slightly after the release of the Outlook Report but fell following Ueda’s press conference. We agree with the move, as there are no strong catalysts for markets to price in an additional hike at the April MPM. Notably, BoJ Board Member Tamura—who is generally viewed as a hawkish member— did not argue for an additional rate hike at this meeting. Near‑term bond‑market attention now shifts to the upcoming Lower House election on 8 February. We continue to think that after the election will be an appropriate timing to buy JGBs on dips (see Japan Viewpoint: Lower House elections - Policy and market implications 20 January 2026). - Tomonobu Yamashita, Rates strategist FX: Govt to address yen weakness via FX intervention Today’s

Systematic, rule-based strategies aimed at extracting an alternative source of returns, e.g. momentum, carry and value. They tend to be highly liquid because the underlying exposure is predominantly in traditional assets which are highly liquid. records.text: 23 January 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 42 Deutsche Bank AG EUR STIR: Terminal rates and tariffs 2026 edition Last year we made the observation that tariff announcements were a key driver of market pricing policy rates in the Eurozone materially below neutral. The impact this time around has been far more muted, consistent with the broader market reaction. Terminal rate pricing rallied 3 bp to price around 6bps of cuts this week. Whilst minor, the price action also stood out in relation to the rebound in near term inflation forwards (which again highlights the contrast to dynamics last April). Recent comments from Lagarde have played up the uncertainty rather than the immediate potential tariff impact to inflation. At the same time, one might assume recent events also indicate upside risks to defense spending. On margin, it does suggest that the former has been more relevant this week at least for the immediate policy path. We remain long TKYM6 where the mild basis widening this week also validates the preference for expressing it in €STR. records.text: rate backup from here, while not currently expected by Citi, could trigger an equity valuation response. The cause would likely be renewed deficit concerns. Tariff Impacts and Fiscal Stimulus — The pending Supreme Court decision on IEPA tariffs poses a risk should the court rule to overturn. The loss of tariff revenues while additional stimulus proposals are considered ahead of the midterms, such as higher defense spending, individual tariff dividend checks, and renegotiation of ACA subsidies, could bring deficits back into investor focus. 2023 Case Study: Long-End Rates Impact — The Q3 2023 episode, where 10-year yields spiked from 4% to 5% as budgetary concerns pushed term premiums higher, offers a relevant case study. During this period of curve steepening, the S&P 500 sold off ~9% as multiples compressed, despite stable EPS expectations. The buyers’ strike was short-lived, long-end yields retrenched, and equity markets ultimately recovered. What to Do? — This depends on time horizons. Anticipating what can disrupt a full- year view can help prepare to capitalize on pullbacks. Shorter term, implied volatility (i.e., VIX) has reverted lower this week and can be a means of hedging this type of tail risk, but we will leave that for our trading strategy colleagues for more specific strategies. records.text: Emerging Asia Outlook The spectre of policy tightening We have penciled in monetary policy tightening in Malaysia and Singapore later this year – notable, given how globally most other EM central banks are generally tilted more towards easing. BNM stayed on hold as expected but sounded more positive on growth; MAS will likely stand pat next week too. US President Donald Trump's reversal over tariffs on Europe over Greenland removes a potential stumbling block to the export cycle, which continues to hold up overall in Emerging Asia. Based on the latest December trade data now available for many major Emerging Asian economies – China, India, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam – our Barclays EM Asia Export Cycle Tracker, which aims to provide a more broad-based and timelier measure of the state of play in the region, indicates that the region’s export cycle remains at still-strong levels overall, broadly rising further following an already visible jump in November. Notably, the latest GDP data released so far in the region suggest output gaps are generally remaining in positive territory in Q4, with the exception of Korea, where it appears the Q3 resurfacing out of the negative zone was merely a one-off. We believe this is underpricing how move the 30y rate can underperform in a large sell-off considering the recent episodes of bear steepening in DM rates. Based on model pricing (as of 1/21/25 close), costless 1y fwd 5s30s and 10s30s bear steepeners have relatively high positive total pickup compared with other structures (Figure 5). We would avoid a 5s30s bear steepener because of the tendency for the 5y to lead and bear flatten in an unexpected growth recovery sell- off. In terms of the strikes, we prefer to push them more OTM than usual because we believe it is more likely for the buyers strike to materialize and the 30y to underperform in an outsized rates sell-off. records.text: European Viewpoint | 23 January 2026 5 FX: EURUSD and EURDKK moves Adarsh Sinha Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Michalis Rousakis MLI (UK) Kamal Sharma MLI (UK) Is US escalation vs. Europe positive or negative for EUR/USD? The EURUSD exchange rate is at the intersection of downside risks to European growth from bilateral escalation (EUR negative) and Europe’s role as the marginal funding source for the US current account deficit (USD negative). Our qualitative assessment was that Greenland developments could help the EUR ( EUR – will it rise to the occasion? 12 January 2026), which was validated by price action early this week: US equities down, US rates up, vol up, EURUSD up. The market reaction was measured vs. April 2025, partly due to diminishing “shock value” but also the eventual de-escalation on Wednesday having likely been the base case for most investors. Still, the consistency of this price action over time is notable. While Greenland implications extend well beyond tariffs, EUR’s response to surprise tariff escalation vs. the EU has been consistently positive. Exhibit 5 shows the average excess return relative to trend following such events has been close to 1% over the subsequent week. There has also been a clear inflection in the FX beta to US rates – higher US 10y real rates is no longer associated with a stronger USD (vs. EUR, Exhibit 6). Third, we turn to simulations with our small macro model of the Euro area, which is a simplified version of the staff’s ECB-Base model. The benefit of this approach is that we can provide a dynamic perspective on the hurdle for policy shifts and consider the feedback from policy changes into the economy. Our framework includes real GDP growth, core inflation and the ECB policy rate, related by so-called IS and Phillips curves, with forward-looking expectations. To best approximate the information set available to the Governing Council, we use the ECB staff projections as a baseline for the macroeconomic outlook. Morgan Securities Australia Limited Global Markets Strategy Global Fixed Income Markets Weekly (Advance version) 23 January 2026 J P M O R G A N AUD/USD FX is up around 10%oya, so is also tempering financial conditions. Following the rate differential channel, BoP data show portfolio flows indeed became more supportive for AUD through 2025 (see 2026 FX Outlook: AUD). We expect this to continue in 1H26 given the benign ACGB supply outlook and comparatively steep curve (the supply outlook, and contrast to other DMs is covered here). Similarly, although geopolitical developments remain highly fluid, the response to them seems directionally easier to call, and we have expected a gradual increase in FX hedge ratios by the local pension fund system. Changes in raw material prices affect consumer price inflation mostly indirectly via production costs, although some relatively unprocessed commodities are part of energy and food categories in CPI. The latter explains the comparatively high content of oil and agricultural commo dities in US headline CPI (LHS figure). For core CPI, the commodity content is relatively modest (in the 0.5% -1% range) 2, with labour and distribution costs, margins and taxes typically being a larger share of consumer goods selling prices. Basing policy on those dynamics would have meant greater easing in mid-25, which would have been a mistake. records.text: Japan Macro Watch | 23 January 2026 3 Rates: No clear message to support the JGB market As broadly expected, the BoJ kept its monetary policy unchanged at the January MPM. The BoJ did not send any signals or outline potential triggers for conducting ad‑hoc bond‑buying operations or funds‑supplying operations against pooled collateral to provide support to the bond market. Following the release of the statement and the Outlook Report, JGB futures fell by roughly 0.3 yen, reflecting the upward revision to the BoJ’s median inflation outlook (all items less fresh food and energy) and suggesting that some market participants had expected the BoJ to signal bond‑supportive operations. The market‑implied BoJ policy rate for the April MPM is now around 0.9%. It rose slightly after the release of the Outlook Report but fell following Ueda’s press conference. We agree with the move, as there are no strong catalysts for markets to price in an additional hike at the April MPM. Notably, BoJ Board Member Tamura—who is generally viewed as a hawkish member— did not argue for an additional rate hike at this meeting. Near‑term bond‑market attention now shifts to the upcoming Lower House election on 8 February. While the latest attack on the Fed did not influence any change to our investment set, it at least affirmed our negative view on the USD (which we maintain with our short USDCAD trade). We are also generally sceptical that investors can fully abandon the greenback and treasuries in the face attacks to the Fed’s independence, at least until poor policy decisions creates a paradigm shift in economic expectations. So, while media mentions of independence are surging (see overleaf), overall credibility has yet to reach extremes. Referencing Figure 3, we can also see the stability of market measures of longer-term inflation in the face of waxing and waning credibility. This leads us to the conclusion that so long as the Fed remains a data driven independent organization, it will ultimately calibrate policy correctively, leading investors to comfortably anchor their inflation outlook. Recent history shows us that the period of transitory inflation eroded credibility, while super-sized hikes in 2022 re- established credibility. For longer term inflation expectations (which are the bedrock with which long yields are built) investors ultimately believed the Fed would eventually get it right. Also the marginal propensity to spend out of the income that is received (not simply recorded by the BEA) will lead to further divergence between income and spending. Consumers typically report the main uses of tax refunds as saving and paying off debts, neither of which count as consumption. This shows through in the data too, with loan delinquencies (on credit cards, auto loans), typically declining from February - April. In our forecasts, we expect a slightly higher spending boost in 1H from the bill. However, delayed spending benefits from refunds and benefits from lower withholdings will also mean some of the benefit is spread throughout the year. Studies have shown that typically around 30-40% of refunds or similar stimulus payments get spent in the first quarter after being received, and given that much of the benefit will go to high-income and older consumers, we expect the marginal propensity to consume could be even lower. The process for selecting candi- dates for a by-election is administered by a panel of the Labour Party’s National Executive Committee and current elected mayors need to seek the express permission from the NEC to be eligible for nomination as a parliamentary candidate. If approved, there is a multi-step selection process including selection interviews for the prospective candidates with the final candiate selected by a ballot of the Constituency Labour Party Members. The difficulty for Mayor Burnham is that the NEC could easily deny permission for him to be nominated as a potential candidate on strategic political grounds. Even if he were to be selected as the Labour candidate for the seat of Gorton and Denton there is no guarantee he would actually win the by-election as polling suggests Labour trail Reform by six points. For now, we think it is too early to price any significant increased political risk premia around a potential Burnham-led challenge to the Labour party leadership into intermediate gilts until there is more clarity around the upcoming by-election process. For all of the undeniable geopolitical uncertainty circling markets, the question that is most pertinent is: why are we not seeing a bigger reaction? The announcement at the weekend that the US was to impose 10% tariffs on seven European countries, with these possibly rising to 25% in June unless an agreement on the future of Greenland is reached, has caused only a limited fall-out. For sure, there were some fairly significant moves in Asia and Europe on Tuesday but FX markets barely moved further once the US opened and even retraced some of the overnight shifts. While many put the moves down to the Greenland effect, one can argue that the sell-off in JGB yields had just as much of an impact on global markets. So where does this leave us? From a core investment viewpoint, exactly where we were on Friday. For sure, tail-risks have increased as a result of the weekend announcement, but they remain tail-risks. The overall fundamental environment is still largely benign, the rest is noise. Growth expectations for 2026 are solid and central banks are expected to adjust rates only gradually. Indeed, only 280bp of absolute rate moves are priced for the G10 in 2026 with not one of the 10 central banks fully priced to adjust rates more than once. We have recently observed that the positive directionality between belly rates and long-end curve shape that had prevailed over the past few years has started to turn negative. Consequently, any further repricing in right tail risks around the terminal rate has scope to flatten the curve and compress long end risk premia. While bouts of JPY-specific risk premium shocks (such as the fiscal-led dramatic bear steepening earlier this week) could still present temporary disruptions to this trend, we think the BOJ’s evolving reaction function will start to see flattening pressure become more pronounced over time. For now, significant relief for this duration risk premium seems unlikely. Fiscal uncertainty will likely persist through the election (likely to be held on February 8) and could extend until the spring budget finalization (end of March, with some risk that a delay of the budgetary process could see uncertainty extend further), even with a LDP victory. Unlike the 2022 Gilt crisis, there are fewer signs that the long-end JGB selloff is causing significant balance sheet strains that would prompt an aggressive BOJ response. With the long-end buyer base hesitant to step in amid heightened volatility, the most probable path to stabilizing the long-end curve steepness may be a moderation of the LDP’s expansionary fiscal policy rhetoric. Over the medium term, the UK experience suggests that it would ultimately take an easing of inflation risks for the market to relax

Yes, we expect three further Bank Rate cuts this year to a 3% terminal rate this year, notably below market pricing. Rising unemployment and falling inflation should allow the MPC to normalise policy, with our estimates pointing to a neutral nominal rate of round 3%. Consistent with this, our optimal policy simulations—which use a small macro model to trace out the path for Bank Rate that best delivers on the MPC’s remit—point to steady cuts ahead. The exact timing of rate reductions will depend heavily on the incoming data. The latest MPC commentary suggests that the Committee could cut at a slower pace than quarterly if the data are in line with the Bank’s projections. Our economic forecasts are weaker than the Bank’s estimates, however, and so we think that the Committee will cut more steadily than the latest guidance implies. As such, we see cuts in March, June, and September as the baseline, although a more drawn-out cutting cycle is possible if the data are firmer than we expect. Avoiding a rapid spike in long-term yields is a clear priority, but an accelerating yen depreciation that erodes household real purchasing power is equally serious. As such, we would not expect the BoJ to increase JGB purchases lightly. One underlying reason for persistent yen weakness and rising long-term rates is the delay in monetary tightening. records.text: rom a theoretical OAS/payup perspective. Of course, one of the problems with the theoretical OAS/payup perspective is that it's, well, theoretical. Investors don't get paid in OAS, and in the interim, the carry on the higher coupon specs is substantially better even after accounting for hedging costs than the carry on the TBA. When we think about the combination of possible changes to help the ease the burdens to refinance along with further improvements in AI and worsening of the deliverable, the real question is simply how rich should specs trade to TBA and what is the right hedging strategy. Looking at spec 6.0s, most of them are profiling around 25 TOAS, 85 ZV, and currently carrying over 4 ticks/month vs duration hedges. While the carry is likely to erode somewhat as the bonds go up the ramp, as simple cash flows higher coupons still provide reasonable value in our minds. Further down the stack the bonds are more like call options, although the payup convexity does not look incredibly attractive. However, we think that the payup convexity may not quite be the way to look at things due to the compositional differences across coupons and implications that has across payups.

(see Leveraging a multi-factor model for hedging FX risk) ▪ Our G10 multi-factor model achieves a simulated historical Sharpe ratio of 1.3 by combining 10 expressions of well-documented FX risk premia, including carry, momentum and value. We use a mean variance approach and a Gerber correlation matrix to derive allocations across USD pairs. Our finding is that the Gerber statistic has indeed historically outperformed other methods of estimating the correlation matrix in the G10 FX universe. ▪ Leveraging this multi-factor approach for hedging equity investments in the G10 universe improves the average Sharpe ratio by 10% over a dynamic minimum variance optimization baseline. records.text: US Economics Weekly23 January 2026 ab 32 Services surveys (Jan) We expect the FRB of Dallas services index remained below zero for the fifth consecutive month in January, down 1.7 points to -5.0. Comments released alongside the FRB of Dallas services survey have recently highlighted uncertainty, interest rates and tariffs as headwinds. See last month's comments here. The FRB of Richmond services index, which is a business activity index rather than a composite, likely improved marginally, up 4 points to -7, after spending ten of the 12 months of 2025 below zero. Thus far in January, the flash January estimate of the S&P Global services PMI was unchanged at 52.5. The FRB of New York services index remained weak, up 3.9 points to -16.1. The FRB of Philadelphia non-manufacturing index rose 17.4 points to -4.2, but continued its weak trajectory — it has only made brief trips into expansion a handful of times since mid-2022. The FRB of Kansas City services index was little changed, up 1 point to 2. Regional services surveys generally moved sideways in December, remaining very weak for an expansion across the board. Our main take-away from the December meeting was a sense of tension between the policy signal which was determinedly neutral and the new staff forecasts and President Lagarde’s description of the macro picture which were arguably more positive/hawkish. The details of the ECB accounts confirmed this tension. Based on the volume of discussion, the Governing Council’s focus seems to have been on the risks to the outlook rather than the hawkish revisions to the projections. There continues to be divisions as to the balance of risks surrounding the inflation outlook. But the Governing Council also see risks (both to the upside and downside) around the growth outlook including several structural questions related to topics such as savings behaviour, a second "China shock”, the impact of AI, and fiscal policy. The details of the accounts support our view of policy. The high levels of uncertainty keep open the risk of a further insurance cut in the near term (a risk we have highlighted for a while now). It also is consistent with our recent decision to push back the expected timing of the first rate hike from end-2026 to mid-2027 as it will take time for some of the structural questions the Governing Council have around the outlook to be resolved. As a result, we are trailing the stop-loss level from 241bp to 176bp (securing 20bp of profits), while setting a new profit-taking level of 46bp (from 96bp). We are setting a trailing stop level as an important point approaches regarding expectations for the outcome of Colombia’s presidential election. Indeed, we view the next few weeks as key for shaping market sentiments around this event, as the results of polls carried out by surveyors perceived as well-established and credible will be released. If the overall results suggest a strong likelihood of a swing of the political pendulum, we expect a new leg of premium compression in the Coltes curve. A move to the right would be particularly beneficial for the Coltes curve as the market would likely price in an improved fiscal outlook. Affordability in Focus: Housing Policy Our policy team sees five pillars of policy change when it comes to affordability: 1) housing; 2) consumer credit; 3) energy; 4) health care; and 5) trade policy. Housing proposals will likely continue to receive attention from investors. Economic impacts are limited barring a substantial decline in the mortgage rate, and our housing strategists see the programs discussed so far pushing sales marginally higher while having little impact on our home price expectations. The tightening in agency mortgages should support other high-quality assets, in particular securitized credit AAAs. Assessing the policy with the highest plausibility, we think that $200bn in purchases from the GSEs would drive mortgage rates down 15bp. It is worth noting that other proposed changes, such as assumability and portability of new mortgages, could increase velocity in the housing market but would also drive mortgage rates higher, all else equal, potentially working against affordability objectives. Retroactively making existing mortgages portable or assumable would likely face considerable legal hurdles. Policies to increase supply could improve affordability through lower home prices, but that would also impair a large asset on the balance sheet of 65% of the country's households. records.text: M Idea 38 Weekly Summary for Overseas Investors Market Recap Spec Monitor As a reminder, we went neutral last week, and when we think about it in the near term, the most likely outcome is some modest spread volatility around these levels. Investors who are long will likely earn carry from improved roll specialness and possible support from a faster-than-expected pace of GSE demand without material profit-taking given a lack of alternative high-quality asset classes and strong technicals. Other positive catalysts include the upcoming release of Basel Endgame, an increase in GSE program size and/or faster pace, or discussion around ending the Fed's MBS run-off. On the other hand, investors who are short are likely looking at valuations in general being too tight without much room for spread widening. Profit-taking, increase in macro risk or vol, further policy changes that are stack-negative, and normalization of rolls could weaken performance. Putting it all together, the outlook for positive excess returns vs Treasuries is still a little difficult given current starting valuations, but we want to reiterate that the marginal buyers (GSEs, REITs, banks in AFS accounts) are likely looking at MBS vs swaps. The latest developments over Greenland have overshadowed the recent news flow surrounding France and PM Lecornu’s last attempt to pass the 2026 budget. As reported by the press, the latest budget concessions might be enough to secure the Socialists’ abstention during a crucial no confidence vote that is expected to follow the activation of Article 49.3, which bypasses the parliamentary vote process. At this stage we do not know the exact deficit target for 2026 which, according to the French PM, would be no higher than 5%. While these latest budget concessions might create upside risks to a 5% deficit target, it’s worth emphasizing that as far as trading of OATs is concerned, the avoidance of elections and the survival of the government are likely to matter more than a less ambitious deficit target, at least in the near -term. Hence, this is a net positive for OATs. The reason we believe this is the case has to do with current cheap OAT valuations vs fundamentals, an indication that a certain degree of political risk premium (cheapness) is embedded in OATs prices. The list of options is broad, and covers areas such as trade in goods, services, foreign direct investment, financial markets, public procurement, trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights, export controls, and more.” Why wouldn’t the EU restrict its retaliation solely to goods? The EU has limited scope to retaliate through goods if energy is excluded. The first line of defence would be the set of tariffs already agreed – and now suspended – in the July deal. But if the EU chose to escalate further, it would need to look beyond goods, which is where the other side of the goods US-EU “imbalance” becomes visible (Exhibit 5). More importantly, retaliation always comes at a cost. Short-term, and assuming services provision is not disrupted, the cost of targeting services rather than retaliating more aggressively through goods would likely be smaller. Europe typically tries to negotiate until the very last minute when things escalate, especially when a potential off-ramp is in place. Hence, we would not expect more than conditional statements to come out of the Emergency EU summit taking place as we write this report. Compared to the RPI fixings market pricing, our bottom-up RPI forecast is 5-10bp higher in Q1, but 10-15bp lower in Q2 and Q3, with the gap widening to 30-40bp in Q4. We think the inflation market could be pricing a positive risk premium around the October Ofgem cap revision, potentially factoring in risks of higher wholesale energy prices next winter. Given the latest spike in natgas futures, 3 and potentially low European gas storage levels after the 2025/26 heating season, the inflation market reaction is not unreasonable (eg, Nov-26 RPI fixing rallied c.25bp since end-December). Also, our own Ofgem cap model could be too conservative on a 6m-12m horizon, and may not fully take into account upside risks from higher wholesale natgas prices should the recent natgas price spike fail to reverse. Still, a c.40bp spread between our bottom- up forecast and 1y RPI market pricing provides a sufficiently wide safety net, in our view, to enter shorts in 1y RPI, part energy-hedged, which we recommend this week (Nov-26 RPI fixing; spot: 334; target: 300; stop: 355). 22 January 2026 43 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: The more things change...

" This marks a shift from its view in 2025 that the acceleration in credit card spending was increasingly due to changes in consumer payment behaviour. The CBT's hawkish surprise is likely to reinforce disinflationary support from the expectations channel. On the demand side, the CBT is likely to announce additional measures to slow the pace of loan growth. The FX channel is still the most important contributor to disinflation and is very likely to remain unchanged throughout 2026; there is both strong willingness (the disinflation strategy, resident de-dollarisation, non-resident inflows) and strong ability (usable FX reserves, a stable-ish C/A deficit trend) to maintain the FX policy stance. Before the 22 January decision, we expected four 125bp cuts in H1 26 and four 100bp cuts in H2 26, for a year- end policy rate of 29%. We now expect seven 100bp cuts over the rest of 2026, taking the year- end policy rate to 30% (CBT Review: Hawkish start strengthens disinflation anchors, 22 January 2026). 23 January 2026 62 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: When noise becomes the leitmotiv

We see a strong case for the BoJ to become more proactive in its tightening cycle. A recent opinion poll found that 45% of respondents cited prices as their main concern, with diplomacy and national security a distant second at 16%. The Japanese government and the BoJ are becoming increasingly sensitive to currency weakness, which is also reflected in a greater repricing of the front-end as the currency weakens. Conclusion: Consider flatteners if the BoJ becomes more proactive In our view, the case for JGB flatteners remains strong from a macro and valuation perspective and has 100bp+ potential, and we see the case for a more proactive monetary policy tightening is becoming stronger. If such a signal emerges at the forthcoming BoJ meeting, we would consider re-engaging in the flattener. In the meantime, we maintain our current short position in the 2-3y sector. Based on these indications, we think the bar for a fresh Moody's positive outlook at some point in 2026 could be somewhat lower than for the other two agencies (albeit less likely in H1, given how recently Moody's upgraded the rating). It should also be noted that Moody's currently rates Italy one notch below the other two agencies. Elsewhere in the periphery, we think scope for fresh positive outlooks in 2026 could be somewhat greater for Spain, Portugal and Greece, given ongoing growth outperformance and consequent downward pressure on debt/GDP ratios. We do not expect a repeat this time, at least not just yet, particularly given Trump has quickly pivoted. records.text: Fallen angels: Duration can cushion the fall. We forecast $20 billion of net fallen angels this year, but many investors view risks skewed to the upside given roughly $590 billion of BBB-rated bonds on negative outlook vs. BB-rated bonds with positive outlook—the largest imbalance since 2020. Ratings migrations tend to be priced asymmetrically: historically, the market has penalized the first signs of deterioration more than the subsequent downgrade that formally pushes a name into HY, while rising stars typically tighten on the upgrade as crossover buyers step in (Exhibit 14). That being said, not all fallen angels are treated equally. HY investor demand appears strongest for long-end paper, which is scarce in a market that has an average duration of three years. While both long-end and intermediate-maturity bonds typically widen on the initial downgrade, we find 10+ year maturities tend to outperform once they land in HY, as the duration bid takes over (Exhibit 15). With nearly 40% of BBB-rated bonds on negative outlook maturing in 10+ years, we think the spread impact from a downgrade wave would likely be more muted than the headline fallen angel risk may suggest (Exhibit 16). French government passes the 2026 budget Fiscal policy has also been in focus in France, where the Lecornu government this week finally passed the 2026 budget, while staying on track to remain in office. Admittedly, the adopted budget delivers less tightening than initially proposed, as the government plans a 5.0% deficit compared with the earlier 4.7%. It is also less business friendly, as most spending-restraint measures were abandoned and the bulk of the adjustment will fall on businesses via tax increases. records.text: idual parties set their own rules. Where the Conservatives have a relatively low hurdle for challenging, the Labour party rules are more stringent. The first point to note is that Labour MPs cannot formally hold a vote of confidence in the party leader.2 Under the previous government, Conservative MPs could submit motions of no confidence which would trigger a leadership challenge. Instead, Labour MPs can only initiate a leadership challenge prior to the annual session of party conference, which is usually held in the Autumn.3 A labour leadership challenge is also a complicated process, assuming the leadership isn’t vacant. At time of writing (23rd January), there is no suggestion that the Prime Minister might resign. A would-be leader needs the support of 20% of Labour MPs (this currently means 81 MPs) alongside either 5% of Constituency Labour Party members or three of the affiliate party structures, of which two must be trade unions and amount to 5% of affiliated membership. As a mayor, Mr Burnham faces the additional hurdle that he needs to seek “express permission” from the NEC to become a candidate for MP .4 If these hurdles were met, an election could be called no-sooner than two-weeks later, although the timeline for any vote would be set by an “independent scrutineer” . History demonstrates three potential paths to an extended period of equity n market broadening: A “catch down” collapse in the valuations of the largest stocks, a broad-based “catch up” increase in valuations across the market, or a market broadening driven by earnings broadening. Our forecast for economic acceleration in early 2026 points to the third scenario as the most likely near-term outcome, and we expect the recent broadening will continue. records.text: M Global Foundation 18 Demand Outlook Euro area EGB demand in 2026 should look broadly similar to 2025, with banks, asset managers and foreign investors providing the bulk of support. For many investors the absolute level of yields or spreads is a significant determinant of demand, but ratings can also play a part. The key headwind is ECB QT: roughly €300bn of 2026 EGB maturities are expected not to be reinvested, adding to the amount markets must absorb (with QT slowing slightly in 2027). Euro area banks should be a major anchor through 2026 as yields, swap spreads and deposit growth stay supportive. Foreign demand has been unusually strong across euro area countries, though Japan’s interest remains modest versus past cycles and reserve-manager demand looks stable. Finally, Dutch pension reforms are unlikely to spark meaningful selling; any reductions should be gradual and concentrated in higher-rated sovereigns, with the transition still supportive for bonds versus swaps. We expect US corporate credit demand to stay healthy in 2026. Our forecast for steeper treasury curves historically supports credit demand: lower front-end yields push marginal buyers out the curve and reduce FX-hedging costs for overseas investors. records.text: Attention now shifts back to the data front Amid this cacophony, the BEA continued to catch up on releases that had been pushed back by delays in data reporting following the federal government shutdown, providing a better picture of how the economy fared in the final months of 2025. The BEA's updated estimate of Q3 GDP growth, at 4.4% q/q saar (Barclays and consensus 4.3% q/q saar), was largely identical to the initial estimate, showing an economy that was boosted by a narrowing trade deficit and robust private domestic final spending (PDFP). As in the initial estimates, gains in PDFP were led by consumer spending, which accelerated 1.0pp to 3.5% q/q saar, with fixed investment flattening following two quarters of solid gains fueled by AI-related capex. The widening shortfall between GDI and GDP speaks to measurement shortcomings Even so, details continue to hint that the BEA's expenditure-side estimate might exaggerate output gains. Gross domestic income (GDI), which is conceptually equivalent to GDP but measured using estimates from the income side of the economy, placed Q3 growth in aggregate output at 2.4% q/q saar, 2pp slower than the GDP measure. This continues a pattern that has been evident for a while now, with the BEA's estimates showing a widening gap between the output measures over recent quarters (Figure 1). Rates at the short end of the curve held relatively stable, but the bond market vigilantes surfaced to push 10YY up from 4% to 5% in a three- month period from the end of July to the end of October ’23. This move was short- lived and unwound entirely by the end of the year. Yet, this gives us a great case study to frame market expectations should a buyers’ strike or term premium pressures resurface alongside the budgetary catalysts noted above. In this three-month window, the S&P 500 sold off ~9% on the back of a 100bps increase in 10YY. Much as we expect this year, bottom-up consensus EPS expectations actually moved slightly higher through the period, confirming a fairly clean long- end rate backup to multiple compression case study here. We get it, a single episode is not as statistically significant as longer-term data analysis of interest rate impacts. The increase is driven by a combination of AI capex, an uptick in M&A activity, elevated refinancing needs, and improving corporate sentiment, supported by lower expected funding costs on the back of more rate cuts and a front-end rally. A major, identifiable source of supply is maturities/refinancing: 2026 IG maturities are expected to be ~$900bn, with maturities remaining $900bn+ through 2028 and peaking at ~$1.1tr in 2028. Lower funding costs are expected to drive more refinancing and opportunistic issuance from issuers that were sidelined when rates were higher. Another key source is AI and AI-adjacent issuance, which we estimate at ~$400bn in 2026, with the clear majority from hyperscalers. records.text: European Rates Weekly 23 January 2026 Citi Research 19 In order to check whether realized vol is a priced risk factor across Figure 19’s strategies, Figure 20 shows their performance when excluding the months where realized vol marked higher. In other words, could we improve on Figure 19’s naïve carry strategies by shutting them down ahead of an increase in realized vol? Across our six strategies, we achieve an average 1.9bp annualized pickup in performance since 1999, with 5s10s30s outperforming naïve carry strategies across the three samples. Since 2023, however, both 5s30s and 5s10s30s have behaved like long vol strategies – i.e., it would have been best to continue running them according to their carry even when vol spiked higher. A possible interpretation is that the episodes where fiscal concerns have driven higher realized volatility have become increasingly more relevant: this goes against the previous paradigm where higher volatility would fuel demand for convexity, flattening the long end. What if we had actually positioned against carry in months where realized vol marked higher? It includes a broad set of potential actions. In the European Commission’s words: “The types of measure which the Commission may take include restrictions on the access to the EU market and other economic disadvantages for the third country involved. The list of options is broad, and covers areas such as trade in goods, services, foreign direct investment, financial markets, public procurement, trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights, export controls, and more.” Why wouldn’t the EU restrict its retaliation solely to goods? The EU has limited scope to retaliate through goods if energy is excluded. The first line of defence would be the set of tariffs already agreed – and now suspended – in the July deal. But if the EU chose to escalate further, it would need to look beyond goods, which is where the other side of the goods US-EU “imbalance” becomes visible (Exhibit 3). More importantly, retaliation always comes at a cost. Short-term, and assuming services provision is not disrupted, the cost of targeting services rather than retaliating more aggressively through goods would likely be smaller.

records.text: The central bank is likely to maintain its SGD NEER policy band settings for now before acting later, though the tone of the January policy statement is likely to tilt more hawkish to lay the groundwork for potential tightening later this year. The stable core inflation print of 1.2% y/y in December, with its signs of still-benign demand-pull price pressures, is unlikely to stir the MAS into earlier action, even if the central bank is likely to raise its 2026 core inflation forecast range to 1.0-2.0% from 0.5-1.5% (Barclays: 1.5%; see Singapore: December CPI – Still little reason to front-load policy tightening, 23 January 2026). That said, we are inclined to believe the MAS will be more circumspect than most market commentators believe – and act later rather than sooner. We believe the MAS needs to get more comfortable around the sustainability of the AI boom – and that it is not going to end with a significant financial market correction that has visible effects on investment and production decisions in the real economy – before the central bank proceeds with tightening monetary policy, especially as there is no urgency from an (demand-pull) inflation perspective. Our base case is thus for policy tightening to only materialise in July – later than the broad consensus of April – via a 50bp increase in the slope of the SGD NEER policy band (from an estimated 0.5% currently to 1.0%; see Singapore: MAS Preview – Tightening more likely later rather than sooner, 8 January 2026).

records.text: o cold temperatures because a significant portion of the flow consists of produced water and associated gas. When temperatures drop below freezing, water can quickly block valves, flowlines, and gathering systems, triggering automatic well shut-ins. Notably, while shutdowns can happen rapidly, recovery often takes several days, so even brief cold spells can have a disproportionate impact on monthly production data. Texas (Permian Basin): the region most sensitive to temperature fluctuations • Infrastructure is not winterized, with limited insulation and heat tracing. • Temperatures around 32°F (0°C) represent a critical operational threshold. • Even brief overnight freezes can trigger shut-ins due to the high water content in produced fluids. • Importantly, once wells are shut in, restarts are not immediate, as surface equipment and flowlines typically require warming and pressure checks before production can resume. New Mexico (Permian – Delaware Basin): moderately better prepared for winter conditions than Texas • More frequent cold nights have led to partial winterization. • Temperatures in the high 20s°F can still cause localized freeze-offs, particularly when midstream systems are affected. • Production losses are typically smaller, but often occur simultaneously with outages in Texas. We see scope for solar strength to continue in 2026 as solar capacity buildout across Europe continues. We think this is reflected in low French summer prices; however, we see further downside to German prices in Q2 and Q3. Nuclear deepening the French discount: French nuclear generation rose 4% in 2025, aided by strong nuclear availability throughout the year. We expect this to continue for much of 2026, but note increasing tail risks of outages, with scheduled 10-year inspections of Paluel 1 and 2 in the coming months and evidence of weather risks impacting plants throughout the last year. Slow and steady demand recovery: 2025 power demand rose 1% in Germany, while French demand remained relatively flat. However, this was a function of lower cooling and heating demand from mild temperatures across Q2 to Q4, rather than structurally lower demand. We expect gradual demand growth to continue across Europe in 2026. French demand is particularly sensitive to cold weather, evidenced by an average rise of 5.5% in Q1 2025. T oday’s news that President Trump has reached a NATO framework agreement on Greenland – along with canceling the February 1 tariffs – is the kind of de-escalation we flagged yesterday as a sign to go back to trading FX fundamentals rather geopolitics. As we said yesterday: “The better trigger for us would be the start of the de-escalation process as behind the scenes dealmaking takes place. This should coincide with a peak in cross-asset vol. This could start during Davos, though timing is tricky. ” Of course, there is some small risk the European readout of events is less optimistic, but we do not think that would derail the de-escalation process from here. If the BoJ were to increase its bond purchases, it would strengthen the effect of monetary easing in terms of interest-rate risk, and it would also be yen- negative. Therefore, our economists are skeptical that the BoJ will take policy action. Governor Ueda noted that the spike in super long yields may have been influenced by temporary factors ahead of fiscal year-end, and also stated that the threshold for what constitutes an exceptional rise in yields would be determined in consultation with the government. Because market participants had been expecting a response from either the BoJ or the MoF, if the BoJ does not move, the focus will likely shift to the MoF. The essence of the recent surge in the super long end is a structural supply–demand mismatch in that sector and—given the heavy reliance on overseas investors—a resurgence of fiscal concerns. Following comments by Finance Minister Katayama, the market has calmed for the moment, but dependence on foreign investors remains unchanged, and a sentiment- driven shock could again carry the risk of a renewed spike in yields. In that sense, supply-side measures by the MoF are necessary, and market expectations for a reduction in issuance appear to be rising. Medium-term outlook: Structural undersupply expected to support prices A persistent structural undersupply has been a key driver of Australia’s house price growth for decades, and we expect demand will continue outpacing supply over the medium term. Australia’s population is projected by the ABS to reach 29-30 million by 2030, implying the need for roughly 0.7–1.2 million additional dwellings. However, new supply is unlikely to keep pace: supply-chain pressures continue to weigh on construction, and approvals remain low relative to population needs. This demand-supply imbalance is therefore set to persist, maintaining upward pressure on prices, in our view. Construction: Capacity constraints limiting growth The construction sector enters 2026 still contending with supply constraints across labour, materials, and productivity. Capacity constraints are binding, with elevated workloads in public and private pipelines placing pressure on available resources and driving cost pressure. Rising input costs and weak productivity continue to hinder the sector’s ability to expand supply at scale, even as demand for housing remains strong. In her pursuit of a “high-pressure economy, ” PM Takaichi prefers to avoid rate hikes as much as possible, yet she also has strong concerns about JPY depreciation. For this reason, unless the trend of JPY weakness corrects, we believe she is likely to continue tolerating a gradual rate hike path going forward. As noted above, we continue to expect additional rate hikes in July and December 2026. The December timing is linked to the shunto cycle. However, the BoJ must also remain mindful of the risk that a prolonged interval between rate hikes could trigger a renewed bout of JPY depreciation. With the Fed likely to halt its own rate hikes by mid-2026, BoJ rhetoric alone will not suffice; we believe the Bank will need to deploy “live ammunition” in the form of actual rate hikes roughly once every six months. A July hike would enable a confirmation that wage increases decided at shunto are flowing into macro-wage data as well as a follow-up on the effects of the previous hike through two Tankan surveys, helping the Bank demonstrate accountability. With respect to the upcoming Moody's decision, our base case would be that the rating/outlook are kept unchanged in April, provided the Lecornu government manages to pass a 2026 budget ( likely by decree) and fresh political turbulence can be avoided (likely requiring tacit agreement from the centre-left Socialists to not bring down the government at no-confidence votes, which appears to be the case at the time of writing). At its October review, Moody's projected France's 2026 budget deficit at 5.2% of GDP: hence, a budget targetting a deficit of 5% (as indicated by PM Lecornu) would likely not imply major changes to the Moody's fiscal forecast profile. At the second Moody's review of 2026 on 23 October, a downgrade would nonetheless be a possibility, especially if fresh political discord arises as the 2027 budget-setting process gets underway. The Moody's negative outlook will have been in place for one year by the time of the October review: while in general agencies commonly wait up to two years between assigning a negative outlook and downgrading, the French fiscal/political backdrop has recently been motivating downgrades of France on accelerated timelines. No one wants the losses of a labor market contraction, and everyone wants inflation to get to 2.0%. Those are currently competing demands. The funds rate can not do much to stop tariff cost-push inflation, but it can risk making a weak labor market too weak. Recall the age-old central banker adage “do no harm.” • Tension in the mandate likely leads to tension in the committee. We expect more dissents and continued debate. • The FOMC delivered another 25 bp rate cut at the December FOMC meeting. That leaves the target range for the federal funds rate at 3.50% to 3.75% at the end of 2025. Next year, we expect two 25 bp rate cuts to leave the target range for the federal funds rate at 3.00% to 3.25%. In contrast, there are early signs of greater political cohesion in Europe as nationalist parties and industrial bodies have, in general, condemned the latest US statements. In the medium term, the resolve for greater strategic autonomy in Europe is likely to be reinforced. More importantly, the probability that such resolve survives changes in government is increasing. records.text: 6 Natasha Kaneva AC (1-212) 834-3175 natasha.kaneva@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 23 January 2026 J P M O R G A N The US blockade on Venezuelan oil exports, which lasted nearly a month, left Venezuela with storage at capacity and prompted PDVSA to cut production in early January. Although shipments of Venezuelan crude have accelerated since the US eased its blockade, the increase has not been sufficient for PDVSA to fully reverse its output cuts. As a result, Venezuela’s crude production fell to some 750 kbd in early January, down from 880 mbd in December. While some oilfields have reportedly begun to restore production in recent days, most areas remain below capacity. Export volumes crashed in early January but have partially recovered since mid-January, when oil trading companies began moving cargoes under US licenses (Figure 14). Sales, however, have remained sluggish, as traders are reportedly struggling to find buyers at their asking prices, prompting them to offer steeper discounts to attract interest. Last week, offers of Venezuela’s flagship Merey heavy crude to US refiners were at a discount of $6 to $7.50/bbl below Brent—still higher than the price of comparable Canadian crude. Given the similar quality and greater availability of Canadian oil, US refiners have had little incentive to switch to Venezuelan supplies. Since Monday, JGB 5s30s has steepened by about 10bp, but the level is still relatively flat at 192bp – well below the 204bp seen in November when the large-scale supplementary budget was being discussed. Hence, we think there remains room for further steepening. In an interview at the end of last year, Takaichi had appeared to show some moderation, in a nod to the bond market. However, now that an election campaign is in view, it has become clear that fiscal-expansion pressure cannot be halted, which makes buying bonds more difficult. Even in a scenario where Takaichi loses the election, the likelihood of an expansionary fiscal policy being implemented remains high. From this April, a reduction in the issuance of super-long JGBs is planned, which should provide support from supply–demand perspective. At the same time, increased volatility from short squeezes could make super-long JGBs even harder to purchase. Because liquidity is now extremely thin, even buying pressure from short-covering could quite easily cause the market to temporarily reverse. No commitment to a direction for rates: Many members (from across the spectrum) stressed that the next move for rates could be in either direction. Risks are becoming more balanced: Before the recent disruption caused by the Greenland situation, several Governing Council members noted that risks were becoming more balanced. Thought on potential new US tariffs: Although this morning Trump has taken the threat of tariffs off the table, we did hear from Lagarde that she expected the impact to be “relatively minor”, a view shared by Villeroy. Nagel was more concerned about the effects of tariffs on growth than he was on the inflationary impact. ▪ DB’s outlook: In our World Outlook we pushed back the timing of the first rate hike from end-2026 to mid- 2027. We think the ECB has been showing signs of a greater willingness to tolerate small deviations in medium-term inflation from target. So, the barrier to a policy response may be higher than previously believed. records.text: US Economic Presentation23 January 2026 ab 6 Source: BEA, Haver, UBS Households: bifurcated, caught between tariffs and refunds Tariff related price pass-through should increase pressure on consumers but we’d expect by spring next year OBBBA stimulus could soften the blow, with a bumper tax refund season supporting second quarter consumption. • The US consumer continues to spend. Spending has slowed, but real spending still grew a solid 2.6% over the last four quarters, despite real disposable income growth rising just 1.5% over the same period. • Households across all income groups expect to be more sensitive to future inflation now than in 2022. At the same time, households are less able to weather inflation. Households below the top 20% of the income distribution have historically low liquid assets. • Equity market wealth in Q2 was an all-time high share of household wealth (37%), and accounted for all of the gains in wealth the last few years. • Hard to get too bearish. In Q2 we expect a ~$55 billion boost to tax refunds, thanks to the OBBBA. Euro Area: Rates Strategy Too much, too soon EUR rates have been caught in geopolitical crosscurrents as a combination of tariff risk and JGB spillovers pivot steepened the curve. Heightened uncertainty should keep rate hike discussion at bay on growth concerns. In EGBs, we discuss the outlook for rating actions in H1. Slow down please, the year has just begun. The US administration has kept the geopolitical news tape whirring at warp speed since the turn of the year with the latest headlines around Greenland and tariffs setting alarm bells in Europe. To add to this turbulence and discussions around a potential return of the 'Sell America' trade , the volatility in long-end JGBs has also reverberated across global fixed income. On back of this tariff versus fiscal tango, curves pivot steepened with EUR2s30s c.10bp steeper before flattening back as President Trump dropped his tariff threat on European nations following a framework deal being reached on Greenland. EGB supply: January deluge almost finished Over the past week syndicated EGB supply volumes accelerated, with a Spanish 10y deal, a new 15y from Finland and an Austrian multi-part deal (a new 10y line and a 25y green tap) for a total of c.€25bn. From a timing standpoint, the Spanish deal came in line with our expectations whereas the Austrian/Finnish deals came one week earlier. With auctions accounted for as well, the DV01 of this week's issuance totalled c.€32mn/bp on our estimates, slowing versus the previous two weeks but nonetheless far above the weekly average close to €20mn/bp we expect for the year as a whole ( Figure 13) . With almost all of January's EGB syndication pipeline complete, syndicated supply for the month has totalled €77.5bn. For next week, we expect some further easing of the issuance burden, with a 20y deal from Germany as the only projected syndication (we do not rule out that Germany could instead place its first syndication of the year later in Q1). Accounting for auctions from Italy and Germany, we expect the DV01 of next week's supply to dip to c. €23mn/bp. We then expect a fresh push above €30mn/bp in the first three weeks of February, with a few long-end syndications anticipated (30y deals from France/Spain/Belgium and a 15y BTP). 22 January 2026 36 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: The more things change...

records.text: Kazakhstan: Monetary policy to remain moderately tight in H1 26 As expected, the NBK stayed on hold at 18% and maintained its hawkish rhetoric. At the press conference after the MPC meeting, Governor Suleimenov noted that with high probability, the policy rate will remain at the current level through H1 26, while further tightening remains on the table if inflation pressures resume their acceleration. By the end of 2025, annual inflation had eased to 12.3%, y/y from 12.9% y/y in September, driven by tight monetary conditions (unsecured loans to slow to 6% y/y, from 7.3% y/y in 11m 25), a temporary pause of fuel and utility prices (until Q2 26), and the strengthening of the tenge. On the estimates of the NBK, the gradual increase of the minimum reserve requirements and mirroring of gold purchases also support disinflation via a reduction of excess liquidity and neutralisation of additional money supply, respectively. However, the balance of risks remains tilted towards the pro-inflation side. Key risks include a broadening of and upward adjustments to VAT by 4pp, to 16%, from 1 January 2026; the further increase of inflation expectations of 1.1pp, to 14.7% in December 2025; and uncertainty about the parameters of quasi-sovereign spending in 2026 that could offset the effect of fiscal consolidation and exacerbate supply-demand imbalances. Alongside that, economic activity remained robust: real GDP growth reached 6.5% y/y and will likely remain about 5% y/y in the next few years

records.text: Ning Sun 22 January 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Emerging Markets Weekly : Adding more quality Our Behaviour Risk Scorecard fell to +4 this week from +12, driven by negative shifts across equities and bonds, while FX remained steady at +2. In emerging markets, our data continues to show accelerating outflows from both fixed income and equities, even as EMFX still attracted inflows, albeit at a slower pace than last week. Part of these FX inflows likely reflects investors unwinding currency hedges as they close long FI and equity positions. Geopolitical tail risks also intensified, highlighted by renewed US efforts to assert control over Greenland, and a sharp jump in Japanese bond yields that sparked a broader global bond selloff amid worries over Japan’s inflation trajectory and fiscal sustainability. While our fundamental view on EM remains bullish, the near -term spike in volatility and rising tail risks prompted us to rotate from long ZARJPY into short USDZAR, and to initiate short USDCNH and short USDCLP positions this week. Last year USD convertible bonds saw a new all-time record for issuance at $130 billion with more than half coming from just three sectors: Software, Utilities and Biotech. We believe this was driven by a confluence of factors including improved equity valuations for small-caps, issuers’ focus on minimizing interest expenses, elevated refinancing needs from the outsized 2020 and 2021 vintages, and relatively elevated equity volatility which makes the embedded option more valuable. Moving into 2026, primary market activity has remained elevated, with January volumes of $3.8 billion already higher than the previous four Januarys, with six business days still left in the month (Exhibit 8). We attribute this strong start to the recent outperformance of small-cap stocks which constitute the bulk of the convertible bond issuer base. For context, the Russell 2000 has outperformed the S&P 500 in every trading session so far in 2026. We expect that convertible supply for 2026 will stay at roughly similar levels to last year because all the drivers remain in place. For credit investors still looking for pockets of upside convexity in a tight spread world, and given our portfolio strategists’ view that small- to mid-caps may be the sweet spot for equity returns in 2026, we think converts can still deliver strong returns this year. The Fed is on hold but remains data dependent. The balance of risks around the two mandates hasn’t changed much since Dec. • Chair Powell’s press conference might be dominated by questions about politics rather than policy. On the latter, however, market pricing creates risks of a dovish surprise. • Investors should watch for Powell’s take on i) the Dec u-rate decline, and ii) the link between robust economic activity and the neutral rate. When in doubt, wait The Fed has indicated that it will keep rates on hold at 3.5-3.75% at its January meeting. The labor market is soft and inflation is elevated. Both are stable, so the balance of risks hasn’t changed. With policy now much closer to the Fed’s assessment of neutral, there is no hurry to act. Especially because the economy is about to get hit with a large dose of fiscal stimulus (see: US growth: above consensus and more front loaded). The biggest surprise in the intrameeting period has been the strength in economic activity. That points to a pickup in productivity growth (Exhibit 1), which has mixed implications for policy. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 222/01/2026 We think EM rates in 2026 can be viewed on a spectrum anchored by three core groups, as defined by the recent examples offered by PLN, CZK, BRL, KRW and COP rates markets (see Figure 1). Secular rate cuts: The first group comprises markets that have a secular easing cycle ahead with Brazil, Hungary and Turkey the best examples. Here, the central banks are running elevated policy rates often well above our estimates of neutral rates and the next moves are highly likely to be cuts. Therefore, curves are inverted and usually trade in a bull-flattening fashion. One good example has been how PLN rates traded in late 2024 and in 2025. While the NBP kept its policy rate high (at 5.75%) for a prolonged period, the market remained convinced that the terminal rate would eventually be lower and the PLN IRS curve remained deeply inverted, particularly in the front end. Despite this, front-end flatteners were consistently profitable in PLN throughout this cycle, at least until the policy rate reached something much closer to the presumed neutral rate (Figure 2). This indicates to us that when markets anticipate a secular rate cut cycle, the eventual size of the easing may be underestimated while the initial timing and pace is overestimated. records.text: Spencer Rogers, CFA +1(801)884-1104 | spencer.rogers@gs.com Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC Global Markets Daily: Credit returns can withstand tight spreads 22 January 2026 | 3:59AM MST Very tight starting corporate bond spread levels have some investors questioning n whether they should be bracing for negative excess returns to Treasuries this year. While historically spreads at these levels have often been associated with negative go-forward returns, there are exceptions. Prior historical episodes when spreads reached ultra-tight levels and returns held n up are instructive. We think 2026 has the potential to be a repeat of 2025, with IG and HY markets still posting positive excess returns despite tight starting valuations. This view is predicated on a still-accommodative macroeconomic outlook, solid n and improving credit fundamentals, subdued durations in the IG and HY markets, and still supportive all-in yield levels. Credit returns can withstand tight spreads With USD investment grade and high yield spreads trading near all-time tight levels (Exhibit 1), many investors have begun to question what this means for returns on a go-forward basis. Despite episodes of tight spreads often being associated with negative returns 12-months out, that is certainly not a foregone conclusion. We look to four other prior periods of exceptionally low spreads over the last 25 years and find that the two other prior episodes that most resemble the current environment saw returns hold up. To that point, when S&P and Fitch downgraded France last year, negative outlooks had only been in place for eight and 11 months respectively. With respect to upcoming reviews by S&P and Fitch we think changes to the French rating/ outlook are relatively unlikely, given how recently they downgraded France. However, risks of fresh negative outlooks could become more material in the event of a sharp deterioration in the domestic political/fiscal outlook (eg, if snap elections were to be held on a fresh government collapse). Regarding Belgium, S&P assigned a negative outlook (AA) last April, while Fitch downgraded the rating to A+ in June. Moody's has had a negative outlook in place since October 2024 (with a current rating of Aa3). This could point towards Moody's being the most likely agency to downgrade the rating at its next review (scheduled for 17 April), given that the outlook will have been negative for 18 months. At its latest review, Moody's stated: "The rating could be downgraded if we were to conclude that the government was unlikely to implement measures that would stabilize the government debt burden" . Ultimately, the Moody's decision is likely to hinge on the agency's assessment of the credibility of the Belgian government's reform agenda: last summer, the government unveiled a package of measures aiming to boost labour force participation, reduce early retirement and rebalance the tax system. Two factors help support the credibility of the FX regime in the short run. First, BCRA dollar purchases. The BCRA has bought more than USD800m since the accumulation program started on January 5, a encouraging pace given unfavorable export seasonality. Second, the widening trend in the external surplus. The 3m SAAR trade surplus is at USD18bn (or ~2.5% of GDP), up from a trough of USD5bn in April 2025, spurred by a record energy surplus. In Central America and the Caribbean region, growth in 2025 mostly ended up beating our expectations, and we think 2026 could remain on a healthy pace. Recent employment data offsets some of these concerns and should keep stable policy expectations well anchored. This stands in contrast with continued rate cut expectations from the Fed, driven by mixed data and possible new Fed leadership. Even lower volatility We have moved to a hiatus period in the central bank cycle within the DM space. With most banks at or near neutral there is naturally much less work to be done to normalize rates. In fact, only the Fed and BOE have any notable cuts expected, while the BOJ is still expected to hike 2x this year. With rates at neutral elsewhere, hikes could be next, especially given low global recessionary expectations. Alas, that tightening has also fallen by the wayside, further lowering policy change expectations. FI volatility has followed suit, something we think supports our carry strategy. Attacks on independence While we have seen many periods of waning Fed credibility, none have actually occurred when independence was at risk. We view declining credibility as investors questioning if the Fed is doing its job. Those concerns are often short lived, however, as an independent Fed will eventually find the correct outcome. However, these spikes have faded equally fast. Implieds, despite some temporary increases, have remained close to the lows of the last few years (Figure 21N e v e r t h e l e s s , i m p l i e d s s t i l l r e m a i n c l o s e t o h i s t o r i c a l l o w l e v e l s a n d w e s e e a l a c k o f c a t a l y s t s t h a t w o u l d m o v e i m p l i e d s f u n d a m e n t a l l y h i g h e r ). In our view, this reflects the fact that Euro area yields are expected to remain in a narrow range across the curve driven by ECB on perma-hold and supply/demand dynamics. We see a lack of catalysts that could move implieds sustainably higher. For instance, during the tightening cycle a sharp rise in inflation and inflation volatility had pushed volatility higher. However, macro volatility remains subdued and thus there is a lack of any fundamental driver of implieds higher. We believe this dynamic is likely to prevail over the coming months and warrants tactical trading in Euro volatility. For the FX market, the critical point is that the BoJ did not adopt a clearly hawkish stance to counter yen depreciation. Policymakers surely recognized the risk that, without a clear hawkish signal, yen weakness could intensify. Given that the BoJ refrained from signaling an early rate hike to stabilize the currency, the government is now likely to respond to yen weakness through FX intervention. USD/JPY initially climbed following Governor Ueda’s press conference, but later fell sharply—from the ¥159.10s to the ¥157.30s—before snapping back to ¥158.5 once. While the price action does not point to outright intervention, the market has begun to price in the risk of action, including the possibility of a rate check, as speculation grows. Today’s market behavior shows notable similarities to Friday, April 26, 2024. On that day, USD/JPY also rose following the BoJ meeting and Governor Ueda’s press conference, only to drop sharply thereafter before recovering quickly. According to Ministry of Finance statistics, actual yen-buying intervention occurred on the next business day, April 29. records.text: 4 Insights CURRENCY SNAPSHOTS AND CENTRAL BANK MONITOR Currency View (Buy, Neutral, Sell) EUR The EUR has appreciated, largely as the flipside of USD weakness rather than greatly improved EUR fundamentals. Real money investors are significantly overweight, but fears of an unwind have subsided for now and they are buying once more. We maintain a long versus EURGBP. CAD Canada’s economy has stabilized with persistently high core inflation, while financial conditions have eased under PM Mark Carney’s major fiscal initiatives. The labour market appears to be improving and given the amount of negative news factored in, we have a positive outlook on the CAD and hold a long against the USD. NOK As a large oil exporter as well enjoying a large surplus in its international investor position, we have been favourable toward the NOK for some time and we maintain a long versus the CHF. AUD The medium-term outlook remains positive for the AUD. Australia is experiencing growth driven by private investment, new construction, and favourable terms of trade. Elevated metals and rare earth minerals are helping mitigate the effects of weaker demand from China. This combined with higher inflation will likely put pressure on the RBA to hike. Altogether, we are constructive on the AUD and maintain a long versus the CHF. NZD The RBNZ still may need to lower rates below neutral to boost the economy, given weakening labour and housing markets. However, a lot of the bad news has already been priced in.

The EU’s acceptance of a unilateral 15% US tariff last summer was the reflection of this attitude. In Davos 2026, Greenland changed this fundamentally. The perceived outrageousness of the demands over Greenland, coupled with continuing insults against Europe from the US leadership, seemed have triggered a willingness to retaliate despite the negative economic consequences this could inflict on Europe. Europe is not ‘weaponless’ . During the week in Davos, Europe’s leadership also found out that regardless of Europe’s economic weakness, the EU economy is still relevant enough to make US financial markets react to threats of EU retaliation (including potentially against the big US digital services exporters). Hence, while Europe has no rare earths to weaponise, its economy and holdings of US assets are still large enough to matter for sentiment in US financial markets. And as long as the US administration has a strong incentive to keep financial markets confident, Europe has this as a weapon, at least until the mid-terms. Nostalgia is not a strategy—how can ‘middle-powers’ survive? records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: TARIFFS AND GROWTH; G10 RATES Show me mode The last geopolitical event to cause any meaningful prolonged market reaction was back in April , with the Liberation Day tariff announcement. As we contemplate another round of US tariffs – this time focused on a number of European countries – the markets’ lack of major reaction is somewhat understandable. For all of the angst following the Liberation Day announcements, the consensus for global growth in 2026 is unchanged from the start of 2025 and up 0.2% from 1st May. US growth expectations for 2026 are 0.2% higher than a year ago and 0.6% above the post Liberation Day panic (Figure 3). Ultimately, asset valuations are driven by growth/earnings expectations and the direction of travel of interest rates, i.e. the discounted value of expected future cash flows. The rest is noise. Geopolitical events can cause growth/earnings expectations and the rate outlook to change but, the proof is in the pudding. It was widely anticipated that moving the US effective tariff rate on imports higher (it has moved from 2% at the start of 2025 to over 14% now) would cause a growth slowdown and/or inflation. Neither has proven true to a persistent extent (at least so far). Hence, the post Liberation Day asset market sell-off proved both unjustified and extremely short-lived.
