This feels like a balancing act, with the market weighing: 1. Higher but stable debt/GDP ratio for Italy vs rising debt/GDP for France from a lower level. This is reflecting in the rating trajectory with both Italy and France converging at the single-A band from opposite directions. 2. Stable and fiscally conservative political environment for Italy vs rising political risks with advancing far-right and increasing likelihood of confrontation with the EU for France, a bit like Italy’s mini-BOT episode in 2018. In addition, memory of political instability in Italy during 2010s is still fresh with the Meloni government just partway through its first term, especially for more conservative investors. For instance, Dutch pension funds hold less than €0.6bn of BTPs vs €58bn of OATs. 3. Lower potential growth for Italy than France due to demographics but better management of related fiscal costs (like retirement age of 67 with increases linked to life expectancy in Italy vs suspension of pension reform that proposed increasing it from 62 to 64 in France). 4. BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH French budget: a different type of budget deal In France, acute tensions over the still-not-approved 2026 budget have abated. PM Lecornu struck a deal with the Socialist party. It is not a deal in favour of the budget per se, but rather an agreement that the Socialist party won’t vote against the PM in a no confidence vote to topple him and his budget plan. A series of no-confidence votes is still very likely between today and early February (starting today, actually), as the PM will deliver the 2026 budget by invoking article 49.3 of the constitution, i.e., bypassing the constitution. Headline risks remain, but we assume they won’t materialize. But remember that the 2026 budget struggle is a re-run of 2025. Political fragmentation hasn’t disappeared, so the 2027 budget, then for a presidential election year, is unlikely to prove easier. For the FX market, the critical point is that the BoJ did not adopt a clearly hawkish stance to counter yen depreciation. Policymakers surely recognized the risk that, without a clear hawkish signal, yen weakness could intensify. Given that the BoJ refrained from signaling an early rate hike to stabilize the currency, the government is now likely to respond to yen weakness through FX intervention. USD/JPY initially climbed following Governor Ueda’s press conference, but later fell sharply—from the ¥159.10s to the ¥157.30s—before snapping back to ¥158.5 once. While the price action does not point to outright intervention, the market has begun to price in the risk of action, including the possibility of a rate check, as speculation grows. Today’s market behavior shows notable similarities to Friday, April 26, 2024. On that day, USD/JPY also rose following the BoJ meeting and Governor Ueda’s press conference, only to drop sharply thereafter before recovering quickly. According to Ministry of Finance statistics, actual yen-buying intervention occurred on the next business day, April 29. records.text: China Two-speed economy persists China’s nominal GDP growth has remained below 4% for three consecutive quarters on weaker-than-expected domestic demand and negative GDP deflator, which we expect will persist. Strength in exports and IP are likely to sustain in 2026 amid the US-China AI and space race and global supply chain reset. Real GDP met target while nominal GDP at near 50-year low (excl. 2020) China's Q4 GDP growth slowed to 4.5% y/y, from 4.8% in Q3, meeting market expectations, and bringing the full year growth to the government target of 5% again. For 2025, net exports added 1.64pp, up from 1.5pp in 2024, contributing to ~33% of GDP growth, the highest share since data became available in 2009 (Figure 1). We estimate consumption contribution rose to 2.6pp in 2025 (52% of GDP growth) from 2.2pp in 2024 with real retail sales recovering to 3.7% from 3.3%, while investment contribution fell to the lowest print 0.77pp (15% of GDP growth) with FAI growth contracting by 3.8%, the first time since data became available in 1992 (Figure 2). Looking at the December data alone, in contrast with the stronger-than-expected export growth which boosted IP growth to stronger-than-expected 5.2% y/y from 4.8% in November (Figure 5 and 6), domestic demand indicators all disappointed the market. The (nearly) inescapable implication is that last year's (expenditure-based) GDP estimates exaggerate gains, the (income-based) GDI estimates understate gains, or some combination of both. Taken at face value, the GDI numbers indicate a profound shift in the composition of income growth over the first three quarters of 2025 (Figure 2). Prior to this year, quarterly gains were generally anchored by employee compensation, which had marched steadily upward over the course of the expansion amid strong gains in payroll employment and elevated wage gains. Much of the rest has flowed to the net operating surplus of the business sector. With job gains having decelerated abruptly in recent quarters amid the policy-induced slowing in immigration, compensation has been fairly flat, after inflation adjustments. Instead, gains in aggregate income flowed to less-familiar components in Q2 and Q3, particularly to "taxes on production less subsidies" . The latter is a broad category of the indirect tax take by various levels of government, including sales taxes, property taxes, and tariffs. As we assess the accuracy of estimated GDP , revisions to the GDI estimates will be worth keeping an eye on in the coming months, including the BEA's revisions to compensation as it folds in source data from the Q3 QCEW estimates in mid-March. 23 January 2026 16 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: When noise becomes the leitmotiv

Recent polling (Fig 1) suggests that Labour will face opposition in the by-election. Reform currently leads in the polls, although the margin is fine (30.0% Reform, 28.3% Labour). We think Mr Burnham has the potential to overturn the gap because 1) at the time of polling, the Labour MP was actually suspended from the Labour Party and 2) Mr Burnham is popular within the party (Fig 4). That said, it would likely be a close- run thing. Reform’s popularity should not be underestimated (see Fig 2). Will higher defence spending be financed by joint EU debt for the first time? Yes, we expect common EU debt issuance to start facilitating European defence spending this year. In 2025, the EU articulated its defence strategy through Rearm Europe Plan-Readiness 2030. The primary objective of the programme is to coordinate the increase in defence spending across EU members and harmonize technology and equipment via joint procurement. Readiness 2030 is endowed with significant financial capacity (EUR 150bn, 0.7% of EU GDP) through Security Action for Europe (SAFE), an EU lending facility to fund member states’ defence spending until 2030. The risk is that Moody's takes a similarly sceptical stance on prospects for decisive fiscal consolidation, and therefore downgrades the rating. For S&P , the agency stated at its review last October that "We could lower our sovereign ratings if Belgium fails to reduce its relatively large budget deficits in line with our current forecasts" . S&P's October forecast profile projected Belgium's budget deficit reaching 5% in 2025, before declining to 4% in 2026 and 3.5% in 2027. We view this forecast profile as optimistic: for context, the European Commission November forecasts project Belgium's deficit at 5.5% in 2026 and 5.9% in 2027. S&P also rates Belgium two notches above Fitch and one above Moody's, arguably increasing the impetus to downgrade the rating. Even so, S&P's negative outlook will only have been in place for 12 months by the time of its next review in April. In that context, we think the path of least resistance could be for S&P to hold off on downgrading Belgium at its first review, with a downgrade likely to come either at S&P's second review of the year (in October) or its first review next year. 22 January 2026 8 Barclays | Euro Area: Rates Strategy

records.text: January FOMC Preview: Further to Go, but Not for a While The January FOMC meeting is likely to be uneventful. The FOMC is set to keep the fed funds rate unchanged at 3.5-3.75% and is unlikely to provide much guidance in either the statement or the press conference about future changes to the policy rate. We expect only minor changes to the statement to reflect the latest data. The FOMC might remove the comment from December that inflation “has moved up since earlier in the year” while continuing to note that it “remains somewhat elevated.” It might also add balance to the description of the unemployment rate, perhaps keeping that it “has edged up” but adding that it “remains low.” We expect that only Governor Miran will dissent this week in favor of a cut, a sharp contrast to the three dissents in the statement and the record seven soft dissents in the dots at the December meeting. During the press conference, Chair Powell is likely to emphasize that the FOMC has just delivered three cuts that should help to stabilize the labor market and is well positioned for now while it assesses their impact, echoing the message from recent Fed commentary summarized in our latest FOMC Chatterbox. Moreover, with fiscal politics back to the forefront, we assess the historical impact of supply events on gilt and Bunds. Trade-wise, we reiterate Euribor steepeners, longs in UK inflation, and opt to keep 30yr gilt-Bund tighteners. Longer-term consequences of geopolitical volatility The rise of fiscal politics as a market driver: This week has served up plenty of reminders that global bond market volatility is increasingly being driven by politics with fiscal consequences while monetary policy and economic fundamentals take more of a backseat. The longer-term consequences of the Greenland confusion. “Greenland” tariffs appear to have come and gone within a week, although the next steps are unclear. Still, there are likely longer-term consequences from the volatility of international relations. One might be to accelerate plans for higher defence spending across Europe, perhaps involving joint borrowing, which could further be used after any Russia/Ukraine ceasefire agreement (see SSA section). We note that the EU has not reversed its cheapening since the tariff reversal. Another might be the need for fiscal policy to help rebalance the European economic model towards domestic demand and away from exports (for more on these themes, see European Economics: Implications of the “Greenland” Tariffs).

records.text: 23 January 2026 US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 4 Could more activist balance sheet views be put into practice? As we have repeatedly noted, it takes a majority of the Committee to set policy, including on the balance sheet. And the Committee has long stated that the fed funds rate is its primary tool to adjust the policy stance – this has been in their consensus strategy statement since 2020 as well as their various balance sheet normalization principles over the past decade. Similarly, there appears to be a consensus on the FOMC to shorten the duration of its Treasury portfolio by moving it towards the universe of Treasuries outstanding. Beyond these considerations, more active use of the balance sheet would run counter to Secretary Bessent’s criticisms of Fed policy. Still, while a meaningful shift in near-term balance sheet policy seems highly unlikely, Rieder might be more inclined than Warsh to use the balance sheet as a tool to respond to future shocks (including market dysfunction), and that should be discounted in curves today. In light of this and the dynamics observed this week, we think the immediate market reaction to a Rieder nomination could be to flatten the curve. records.text: end of monetary policy cycles in EM are accompanied by FX weakness, as EM central banks tend to ease policy until pressure starts to build in their own currency. Once FX weakness starts to build up, a negative feedback loop can develop between depreciation and inflation, prompting EM central banks to hike rates to break this feedback loop. During this cycle, however, this behaviour has changed. The examples of the CZK, KRW and even COP (Colombia’s central bank is the only one we currently expect to hike in 2026) show that FX can remain stable through end-of-cycle bear-steepening in rates. Global USD weakness and inflows into EM are the main culprits for this changing FX-rates relationship. Instead of FX, this time around the main triggers for end- of-cycle steepening seem to be positive output gaps (e.g Colombia), domestic inflationary pressures (e.g. Czech Republic) , a depressed level of rates (e.g. in Singapore) and/or continued fiscal spending (e.g. in South Korea). KEY MESSAGES We think EM rates can be analysed in three groups depending on where the countries are in their policy cycle. We use recent examples to create a framework that may guide rates trades in each group. For the first group, still in a secular rate-cut cycle, front- end flatteners may perform well. We find the market tends to underestimate the eventual depth of the cycle. In the second group, an end-of-cycle environment with no immediate prospect of rate hikes should offer good carry trades. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 13 Summit fever | Hedging the Minsky moment with long 0DTE puts THEME 2: Thin air, thick tails Fig. 1: US retail participation in short-dated options trading has skyrocketed • Stability breeds instability. Lower volatility can fool investors into taking greater risk, sowing the seeds for volatility to return in earnest. This dynamic is at play in the US options market where volatility selling leaves dealers with large long gamma exposure locally, suppressing realized volatility. Low realized volatility makes the volatility risk premium attractive, drawing further volatility selling. • Dealers’ gamma is highly spot-dependent though, and any exogenous shock can move the market and lead to much higher realized volatility. • The explosion of retail-driven volumes in US short-dated options is a new feature of the US market ecosystem. At the index level, these flows tend to be selling implied volatility to generate carry. • Systematic buying of 0DTE puts can offer an attractive hedging strategy, as low realized volatility in normal conditions depresses implied volatility (‘cheap hedge’) but shifting gamma dynamics offer convexity in stressed markets. France: a business-unfriendly budget is the price of having a budget at last Lacking a majority in the National Assembly, Prime Minister Lecornu ultimately decided to invoke Article 49-3 of the Constitution to force passage of the 2026 finance bill. Given the remaining steps in the parliamentary process, this means that, unless a motion of no confidence is adopted, France should be operating under a formal budget from the first half of February. Importantly, since the Socialist Party’s tacit support has been secured, we expect the no- confidence motions tabled in response to the activation of Article 49-3 to fail, and we therefore expect the prime minister to remain in office for now. From a fiscal perspective, securing the Socialists’ backing has come with clear costs. It required a meaningful reduction in the planned consolidation effort, with the 2026 deficit target now set at 5.0% of GDP rather than the initially projected 4.7%. It also led to a shift in the composition of the adjustment, as the government financed spending-side concessions to the Socialists through tougher taxation on businesses. records.text: days, and 193% higher on month-ends than other days. Against this market behavior backdrop, several intriguing questions emerge. In this report, we focus on whether the intra-month seasonality in activity can also be seen in price performance. To test this, we analyze intra-month seasonality in forward real rates and CPI zero-coupon inflation swaps (ZCIS), focusing on event windows rather than half-month blocks that we used in our previous seasonality analysis on nominal Treasury yields, as TIPS market trading patterns – used here as a proxy for inflation‑linked market behavior – indicate that activity is overwhelmingly concentrated around these specific event dates. How do we test for intra-month seasonality in inflation markets? To capture these dynamics, we apply a multi-seasonal trend decomposition using LOESS (MSTL) (see below for methodology) on changes in forward inflation swap rates, nominal swap rates, and implied real swap rates (defined as the nominal swap rate less the equivalent ZCIS), using closing levels data going back to 2011. We focus on forward swaps to minimize the impact of inflation seasonality on carry, and we segment moves on key days (CPI/NFP/auctions/month- end) and between them. The price action of EU since 19 December, when the EU leaders opted to finance the next round of Ukraine support with more joint debt instead of using the frozen Russian assets, followed by the latest episode around Greenland, has provided a glimpse into what more supply could mean for EU’s curve. Since late December 2025, EU’s curve has steepened versus swaps with long-end swap spreads widening up to 8bp. The EU also underperformed most EGBs during this period, even despite the recent retracement on the back the apparent cooling of US-EU tensions. This highlights the risk of more supply to EU swap spreads. The more successful it becomes and the more loans it provides, the higher its issuance needs will be (recall, nearly all its supply is net issuance that price- sensitive investors need to absorb). If the increased net supply pushes EU’s funding costs above EU sovereigns, this erodes the economic argument for the member states to fund their defense spending using EU loans. In other words, elevated use of EU to fund defense spending risks it becomes a victim of its own success. Fiscal deficit expansion: While markets have started pricing in higher term premia in part due to renewed fiscal concerns, we are more sanguine about actual supply risks for G4 government bonds. For Japan, a recent focal point of market jitters, our economics team believes the country's fiscal position is structurally improving, supported by the recovery in nominal GDP growth. Moreover, fiscal headlines are unlikely to translate one-for-one into materially higher market JGB issuance. Currency dynamics: We expect USD funding to become cheaper relative to local-currency funding, as our economics team anticipates further Fed easing in 2H26. records.text: nother thing to keep in mind with 2026 being an election year, a midterm election year, it will be very interesting from a congressional perspective. Typically in midterm election years, the legislative window, which is the timeline to pass bills, is significantly shorter. So once we get to late spring and midsummer, I think you are going to see a lot of legislative activity start to dry up as members of Congress are focusing on their own re-election bids in November. And so a lot of the legislation that we will see on Capitol Hill will start to slow off as we get into the summer. Ultimately, to your question, I think the President feels more emboldened really than ever, both to act on his domestic and foreign policy agenda. I think the pace will continue and, if not, it could accelerate in some circumstances, particularly as the President is looking to connect with voters on affordability issues ahead of the midterms. Moving further out, using the same methodology shows that the 1yf 5y term premium of 94bp is also higher than the historical average of 70-85bp though, by a smaller margin. At the very long end, the market-implied term premium of about 180bp is in line with the simple historical averages though this is quite sensitive to the sample period. For instance, if we were to exclude the ZLB episodes, the average slope drops to about 130bp, and excluding both high and low fed funds scenarios, it drops to 145bp. The flip side is that the fiscal profile is worse today than that on average over the past forty years. Whether the long end is mispriced (depending on how concerned one should be with the fiscal situation), the front end is, in our view. We therefore continue to recommend being long 3y USTs, and this extends to our 3s30s yield curve steepener recommendation. The Treasury refunding is coming up and the outcome should result in a steeper curve. There has been some speculation about potential cuts to issuance at the long end. We await further info beyond JPY rhetoric, but see an increasing risk of the next hike coming before our base case of July. • The BoJ wrapped up its 22-23 January monetary policy meeting (MPM) with policy rates unchanged at 0.75%, as widely expected. It also maintained its guidance stating that it will "continue to raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation [...] in accordance with improvement in economic activity and prices [...] given that real interest rates are at significantly low levels. ” • In the quarterly Outlook Report’s economic projections, the real GDP growth forecasts for FY25 and FY26 were revised upward, while the FY27 forecast was revised downward. Market pricing has created room for a dovish surprise More substantively on the policy outlook, we expect Powell to remain strongly data dependent and emphasize a meeting-by-meeting approach. But we think risks are skewed toward a dovish surprise, simply because markets are pricing less than 10bp of cuts cumulatively over Powell's last two meetings as Chair (March & April, see Exhibit 2). Markets will be sensitive to the extent to which Powell leans into the decline in the u- rate in Dec, or downplays it as just a single month's worth of data. Relatedly, we are curious whether Powell will reiterate his tolerance for modest further increases in the u- rate. In December’s presser, Powell said that the policy stance after 75bp of cuts should “enable the labor market to stabilize or [the u-rate to] only kick up one or two more tenths”. The 4- week moving average fell 3K to 202K. For our projection this week, we had pencilled in a smaller NSA decline for this week off the back of a smaller NSA rise in the prior week compared to last year, assuming that a smaller inflow would be paired with a smaller outflow. We wrote in our preview that a downside risk to our projection was a larger NSA decline in claims than we expected, leading to a smaller seasonally-adjusted rise. records.text: 23 January 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 10 Deutsche Bank AG Fixed Income Blog Fed chairs and flatteners Despite focus this week on the potential for global investors to reduce exposures to US assets, US term premia have declined on net. The US is the only G10 country with lower TP on the week (Figure 16). A possible explanation is the surging odds placed on Rick Rieder being selected as the next Fed chair. In line with this, there has been a strong intraday correlation over the week between the 5s30s government bond spread in the US relative to the UK/ EU average, and the Polymarket odds on Rieder (Figure 17). Why would Rieder be a flattener? First and perhaps foremost, by simply not being Kevin Hassett or Kevin Warsh, the two leading candidates over recent weeks. Both could be viewed as steepeners through higher term premia, albeit for different reasons. Hassett is generally seen as quite close to President Trump, potentially leading to Fed independence risk premium. Warsh has long been hawkish on the Fed’s balance sheet, arguing for more limited and less active use of it as a policy tool, views that if put into action should boost term premia through the duration channel. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 The effective tariff rate and high-frequency container traffic We continue to expect that the effective tariff rate will edge up to ~16.0% The Trump administration imposed additional tariffs on trading partners as of August 7 that pushed the effective tariff rate higher to 16.0%. Since then, negotiations with three of the US's largest trading partners – Mexico, Canada, and China – continue to proceed on a separate track. There have been recent announcements regarding both China and Canada. In addition, Section 232 reviews on trade in semiconductors, lumber, and pharmaceuticals, among others, remain ongoing. We expect that the effective tariff rate will remain around 15-16% in 2026. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on the legality of IEEPA tariffs in early November and we await a potential ruling, which could come any day that the court is in session. Given the calendar for the court and the lack of decision in January so far, if no decision is published on January 23, the earliest date for a decision to be released will be February 20. If IEEPA tariffs are invalidated, the effective tariff rate may move lower temporarily as the administration uses other trade authority to reconstitute its tariff regime. See here for more detailed views. Tariff receipts by the US Treasury continue to rise, with the rolling 63-day annualized customs and excise deposits at the Treasury at $391bn. We believe that while the BoJ is preparing for rate hikes, it is not necessarily in a hurry to implement them. Brun-Aguerre, 20 Jan, following the decision to cancel budget discussion in the house, arguing no compro- mise was in sight among MPs, PM Lecornu stated his intentions to invoke article 49.3 to secure the passage of the 2026 budget. This procedure allows the budget law to be enacted without a parliamentary vote, unless MPs bring forward a motion of no confidence and a majority supports it, an outcome that would bring down both the bill and the government. In practice, article 49.3 will be used three times: for the income part, the spending part, and for the whole budget, meaning various motions of no confidence are likely to be triggered through this process. However, the bar to get a majority on the confidence vote is high, as the government made further concessions to the centre-left Socialist Party, and as a result, they argued they would not vote in favor of any coming motion of no confidence. Therefore, we expect the government to remain in office, with the budget possibly to be enacted by mid-February 2026, targeting a deficit of ~5% for the year. At the time of writing, PM Lecor- nu has passed the expenditure section of the 2026 budget using Article 49.

records.text: 12 Global Economic Weekly | 23 January 2026 Medium-term outlook: Structural undersupply expected to support prices A persistent structural undersupply has been a key driver of Australia’s house price growth for decades, and we expect demand will continue outpacing supply over the medium term. Australia’s population is projected by the ABS to reach 29-30 million by 2030, implying the need for roughly 0.7–1.2 million additional dwellings. However, new supply is unlikely to keep pace: supply-chain pressures continue to weigh on construction, and approvals remain low relative to population needs. This demand-supply imbalance is therefore set to persist, maintaining upward pressure on prices, in our view. Construction: Capacity constraints limiting growth The construction sector enters 2026 still contending with supply constraints across labour, materials, and productivity. Capacity constraints are binding, with elevated workloads in public and private pipelines placing pressure on available resources and driving cost pressure. Rising input costs and weak productivity continue to hinder the sector’s ability to expand supply at scale, even as demand for housing remains strong. Private construction rose by 4.7% in 3Q25 relative to 2024 levels, offsetting a fall in public construction after 4 years of strong growth. records.text: M Idea 2 Tax refunds: Adding fuel to the fire Retroactive OBBBA provisions should lead to high tax refunds This week's data on October and November personal income and spending showed continued divergence between spending and income. Real personal spending rose 0.3% m/ m in both months, while real disposable personal income was slightly down, on net, over the period. The saving rate, at 3.5% in November, is now two percentage points below its peak in April. As we discussed last week, consumption is now overshooting its wealth- implied target, but given our outlook for favorable cyclical conditions, we think this can continue. An important near-term factor for both income and consumption in 2026 will be tax refunds. We typically think of labor income as the main driver of consumer spending, but this year taxes and transfer payments will also be important drivers because of the changes in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). The OBBBA included many consumer tax cuts that were retroactive to fiscal year 2025: deductions for overtime, tips, seniors, car loan interest, and an increased SAL T cap and Child Tax Credit. Since withholding tables were not changed last year, consumers will receive the benefit of these provisions in refunds over the next few months. We expect these new fiscal provisions along with some potential underlying increase to boost refunds by $40bn to $70bn from last year's. Retail sales grew 1.0% m/m in November, accelerating from 0.5% in October and surpassing consensus expectations (per Bloomberg) of 0.3%. Gains were broad-based and spread across most categories, likely boosted by Black Friday sales, including furniture (2.3% m/m), healthcare products (2.2%), office materials including cell phones (4.1%), and "other goods" which includes department stores (2.0%), apart from supermarket sales (1.0%). The services sector was roughly flat (-0.1% m/m, versus expectations of +0.1%), interrupting nine consecutive months of growth (with October being revised upward from 0.3% to 0.4%). Industrial production was flat (0.0% m/m, expected 0.1%), in part dragged by mining. As a result of all the above, the BCB's monthly GDP proxy (IBC-Br) grew 0.7% m/m, from -0.1% in October, surpassing expectations of 0.4%. All in all, we see some modest upside risk to our preliminary forecast for Q4 25 growth of 0.0% q/q (1.7% y/y), though probably not enough to sway our 2025 GDP growth forecast of 2.3%. This is not to say that we believe $200bn in purchases of agency mortgage-backed securities will lead to a 100bp reduction in the 30-year fixed mortgage rate. It is standard practice in the economic literature to introduce shocks of a reasonable magnitude, and readers can scale those effects up or down (see here for more detail). The simulation suggests that growth in real GDP rises by about 0.1-0.15pp three quarters after the -100bp shock to the mortgage rate and the unemployment rate falls by about 0.05pp (half a tenth). The decline in mortgage rates produces a minimal boost to inflation, a trivial increase in the 10y US Treasury yield, and a 5-6bp increase in the federal funds rate. On net, the results of the simulation look like a (very small) aggregate demand shock.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 US GDP tracking: 4Q GDP at 2.1% Our tracking of 4Q real GDP growth rose 0.3pp to 2.1% q/q annual rate, reflecting new 3Q GDP revisions along with new October and November data on consumption and prices. Our estimate of 4Q consumption growth rose 0.3pp to 2.6%, reflecting faster services spending than we had built in. The Atlanta Fed estimate inched up a tenth to 5.4%, estimating less weakness in residential investment after the October construction spending data were reported. In their GDP tracking, the government sector contributes about 1 ¼ point more to growth than it does in ours: we are assuming that the federal government shutdown weakened output. Also, we appear to expect a larger reversal in trade flows later in the quarter, which is worth another ½ point to the difference between ours and theirs. We are estimating a slight drag from inventories versus their 1pp positive contribution. And we also assume less strength in consumer spending on services: they're expecting +3.3%, a modest slowing from 3Q; we are estimating 2.9% growth. The NY Fed GDP nowcast rose 0.1pp to 2.7%, mostly because of last week's retail sales report. Sources: BoJ, BNP Paribas Fig.1: Median of BoJ policy board members’ forecasts Unexpected dissent: The Bank of Japan kept the policy rate at 0.75% at Friday’s meeting, as expected. But board member Hajime Takata’s surprise proposal to lift the rate to 1% only a month after the last hike has added weight to the view that the pace of hikes might accelerate. The tone of the Outlook Report released alongside the decision was not particularly hawkish. The projections now incorporate the impact of the supplementary budget introduced at the end of last year, and as such the growth outlook for FY2025 and FY2026 was revised modestly upward. The forecast for FY2027 was slightly reduced, reflecting the fading effect of the fiscal package. The language describing the risk balance for growth was changed from “skewed to the downside”, as seen in the last Outlook Report in October, to “generally balanced” this time. This had been widely expected because the decline in downside risks to the economy was one of the key rationales behind the December rate hike. records.text: JGBs in 2026: A Narrow Path to Modest Relief JGBs were the clear G10 underperformer in 2025 as we expected. This underperformance stemmed from the BOJ’s gradual but sustained tightening as well as rising fiscal and policy uncertainty following the election late last summer. Looking to 2026, while our economists’ baseline argues for a more balanced outlook for Japanese rates, we had argued in our 2026 outlook that near-term risks remain tilted to the bearish side of our baseline given policy risks, while the balance of risks appears more two-sided in the back half of the year. Recent developments have confirmed this view, with back-end yields reaching multi-decade highs, approaching G3 peer levels, and real forward rates nearing the upper end of their historical ranges (Exhibit 1). Fundamentally, we see our economists’ baseline forecasts as consistent with a moderation in JGB yields by year-end. Our baseline forecast is for 10y and 30y JGBs to end the year at around 2% and 3.2%, respectively. But in the near term, market focus will remain squarely on the interaction of fiscal and policy risks with ongoing demand/supply imbalances at the long end of the curve. On the demand side, while the MOF announced reduced long-end issuance in its recent plan (Exhibit 3), this has been outweighed by the continued decline in demand from Japanese lifers, who have most recently been net sellers of long-end JGBs in December (Exhibit 4). In particular, the contraction in infrastructure widened from 12.1% in November to 15.1% y/y in December, hitting an almost six-year low. Such a sharp slowdown, in our view, was partially due to the developments that fixed asset investment statistics have become increasingly rigorous, and the clean-up of inflated data has led to a nominal decline in FAI growth. Moreover, we think the rapid deterioration also reflects the local governments' lack of funding given the payback from the earlier front-loaded LGSB issuance and slumping land sales revenue. For context, land sales revenue is on course to fall to ~CNY4.2trn in 2025 from the peak of CNY8.7trn in 2021 and ~CNY4.8trn in 2024. Moreover, manufacturing investment remained in contraction for the sixth consecutive month, posting a decline of 9.2% in December. • Property investment fell 35.8% y/y in November, a record drop (Nov: -30.3%), and property sales remained deep in contraction, declining 15.6% y/y, still below the level before the policy pivot in September 2024. records.text: United States: Inflation Markets Seasonality in forward ZCIS and real rates The US inflation market tends to display notable intra-month seasonality in trading activity. We examine whether the same seasonality can be seen in price performance and find compelling patterns in inflation swaps around auction dates and month-end rebalancing. This is a reprint of United States: Inflation Markets: Seasonality in forward ZCIS and real rates, published on 21 January 2026. Summary • Forward real rates tend to rise at the start of each month in the run-up to auction dates, then• fade into month-end. The pattern is most pronounced in the belly (eg, 2yfwd3y), consistent with that segment’s liquidity and duration/forward mix. • ZCIS seasonality is front-to-belly led and directionally opposite: ZCIS typically decline into• auctions and rise into month-end. • Weak auctions (bigger tails/lower bid-to-cover) are associated with higher real forwards and• lower ZCIS on the day; between auctions and month-end, dealer-heavy allocations correlate with lower real forwards and higher ZCIS. • Larger index extensions line up with real rate rallies at month-end; impacts on ZCIS are• muted, and extensions have limited explanatory power between auctions and month-end. A more nuanced look at inflation market seasonality As part of our effort to deepen understanding of systematic patterns in the US inflation market, we look into whether intra-month seasonality is something to be expected. Most importantly, he will continue to emphasize that he remains focused on successfully completing his Congressionally -mandated job of achieving price stability and maximum employment. As he noted in response to a question about his legacy to close his last press conference, “I really want to turn this job over to whoever replaces me…with the economy in really good shape. That’s what I want to do. I want inflation to be under control, coming back down to 2 percent, and I want the labor market to be strong. That’s what I want. And all of my efforts are to get to that place.” That said, while not a base case, we do see recent legal actions as raising the potential for Powell to stay on as a governor. Will Spain outgrow the 2.2% consensus expectation? Yes, we project 2.4% growth this year in Spain, again above the Bloomberg consensus of 2.2%. The Spanish economy again outperformed the rest of the Euro area notably in 2025, and investors are watching to see whether the economic resilience will continue. Fiscal policy has been prudent, and is on track to deliver the first positive primary budget balance in 19 years, and the European Recovery Fund continues to support investment. Employment continues to grow robustly, underpinned by continued immigration. We expect real consumption to grow about 3% this year, on the back of strong real disposable income growth and a firm labour market. Spain is also going through structural transformations, with an increasing share of high value-added services (including professional services, finance and IT) and relatively fast adoption of AI in its business sector compared with its European peers. Regardless of the result of the election, the likelihood of a cut to the consumption tax rate has risen. The estimated cost of ¥5trn annually is not a problem in any one fiscal year. In FY3/27 in particular TDB outstanding is due to decline, and the MoF is moving to begin issuance of variable-rate JGBs in January-March 2027. Thus no other funding sources will be necessary. However, even if the cut is proposed as a temporary measure, political parties are likely to advocate for the continuation of tax cuts ahead of future elections. Effectively any cut would therefore be permanent and cause a budget deficit of 0.7%–0.8% of GDP (ignoring the acceleration of growth resulting from the tax cut). records.text: European Rates Weekly 23 January 2026 Citi Research 9 The long and winding route to more joint debt The Treaty on the European Union (TEU) and the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) discuss defense and security extensively. TEU Article 24 states that EU’s competence with regards to “common foreign and security policy shall cover all areas…including the progressive framing of a common defense policy that might lead to a common defense” . TEU Article 42 lays out in more detail the provisions of EU’s common security and defense policy, including the requirement for decisions relating to defense to be reached unanimously by the EU Council. This requirement of unanimous decision does not prevent the EU from taking decisions that have military or defense implications. However, the main constraint on using the EU budget to finance defense/military spending is in Article 41(2) that prohibits charging operating expenditure that arises from “operations having military or defense implications” to the EU budget. This is the main reason why SAFE is a loan programme. Similarly, this is the reason why the EC’s proposal for the 2028-34 MFF – which includes Catalyst Europe, a €150bn of loan facility that can be used for defense, energy, or strategic technology investments – only offers loans. In a speech earlier this week (20 January), the position seemed to subtly change from one of protest to one of acknowledgement that fiscal decisions are indeed in hock to the bond markets while suggesting he had a plan to provide “reassurance to bond markets”. However, the market’s impression that a Burnham premiership could mean significantly more spending and borrowing is unlikely to change. A long way to go: The gilt sell-off on the news may not have legs, however. There are multiple hurdles before this could become a reality: First, Burnham has to secure the Labour nomination for the by-election (and Bloomberg headlines later on 22Jan26 suggest he may be blocked from doing so), then he would have to win the by-election (against a likely strong challenge from Reform), then he would have to find a way to instigate then win a leadership contest. The sell-off may not last. Thursday’s price action in gilts is yet another reminder of its fiscal sensitivity and the risk to gilts from any eventual leadership challenge. It might trigger some lightening of positions but, for now, it is most likely to only inspire a short-lived sell-off in our view. Global term premia are up sharply today on geopolitical tensions and spillovers from Japan. In the US, the increases have been in real term premia, as the forward breakeven curve is little changed. To gauge where the moves leave things, the chart below looks at a measure of real Treasury term premium, which following our standard approach is calculated as the front-end-hedged slope of the TIPS curve. Relative to the post -2004 period over which TIPS have actively traded, real 10s30s TP today sits at all -time highs (dark blue). But for perspective the chart also includes “backcasts” of this measure to the earlier pre -TIPS period (light blue). To do so, we regress TIPS BEIs on nominal yields, CPI, oil, and the S&P 500 over 2004 -present. We then use these coefficient estimates and values of the explanatory variables in the earlier period to construct TIPS yields and, by extension, real TP going back to the late 1970s. The key takeaway from this simple exercise – which admittedly assumes stability in correlations amongst the variables – is that, while real 10s30s TP today sits at a historic post-TIPS high, it does not look nearly as stretched relative to a longer history; it is near late -1990s levels and substantially below levels reached in the 1970s a

records.text: US Economic Presentation23 January 2026 ab 37 Source: BEA, BLS, Haver, UBS What next? The expansion rests on narrow support, driven by AI underpinning the expansion. In 2026 we expect tension between tariff pass-through and fiscal support to drive the economic outlook. However, if the AI momentum in investment or support for equities falters, the expansion itself would be at risk. The FOMC will need to confront these tensions too, with tensions in the mandate likely leading to tensions in the committee. We expect dissents, but see the Fed funds at 3% - 3.25% by the end of 2026. After the economy goes through a period of adjustment, we expect a pickup in the pace of growth. Brisbane and Perth prices have risen 44% and 58%, respectively, over the past three years, compared with gains of 21% in Sydney and just 7% in Melbourne. This divergence reflects a combination of relative affordability, strong interstate migration, state-specific policies, and post-pandemic structural shifts, including greater acceptance of remote and hybrid working. We expect Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide to continue outperforming in 2026, although growth should gradually converge toward more typical rates as affordability constraints tighten. In contrast, Sydney and Melbourne are likely to see only modest gains, constrained by serviceability pressures, higher starting price points (in Sydney), and more normalized listing volumes. records.text: European Rates Weekly 23 January 2026 Citi Research 20 Given that all strategy designs so far only look at the sign of the monthly change in realized volatility, our final question is whether it is possible to filter out some noise by selecting a monthly change threshold below which carry continues driving positioning. We therefore modify the design of Figure 22’s strategies so that we position against the carry signal only as long as realized vol at trade inception is at least 10bpv higher than the previous month’s. Figure 23 shows no average improvement across our six strategies in the longer sample, but 11bp in the most recent one. While the improvement in 2s10s, 5s30s, and 2s10s30s is most pronounced in the most recent sample, we interpret the results as offering modest evidence that imposing a threshold on the monthly change in realized vol improves dramatically our results. records.text: US Economics Weekly23 January 2026 ab 5 Supreme Court seems skeptical of Cook removal The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in the case now referred to as Trump v. Cook or Docket Number 25A312 this morning, see the full transcript here. The hearing was the next step in the Court’s consideration of whether Lisa Cook can continue to serve as a member of The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and by extension, the Federal Open Market Committee, while allegations of mortgage fraud against her leveled by the current administration are considered. As a reminder Governor Cook’s term as governor is not set to end until 2038. For the American Bar Association’s history and summary of the case see: this link. Reporting from the WSJ, see here, suggested the Justices expressed skepticism on the administration’s removal of Cook and they noted that none of the justices expressed sympathy for the arguments made by Solicitor General of the United States Sauer. In the arguments, the justices probed the question of whether notice and hearings were required to remove Cook from her position (in other words, was due process followed); the evidence of harm should they grant or not grant the stay; interpretation of the "for cause" standard for removal in the Federal Reserve Act; and the overarching question of whether this is a decision for the courts to make at all. Takaichi has cited the use of non-tax revenues and the streamlining of special tax measures and subsidies as potential funding sources. However, she has provided nothing concrete, merely stating that discussions will be accelerated within the National Council to be established after the election. This implies potential for a hold-off and/or changes in the scale/target of the tax. Meanwhile, the CRA has proposed establishing a JPY500trn sovereign wealth fund and using its investment returns to finance the tax cut. In the draft proposal originally envisioned by Komeito, public financial assets such as the GPIF, the BoJ (through its ETF holdings) and the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account would serve as the funding sources. However, there are numerous challenges, including how to handle FX intervention funds, governance issues and the appropriateness of using highly volatile market returns as a permanent revenue source for tax cuts. records.text: European Rates Weekly 23 January 2026 Citi Research 7 Probability of new EU programme for defense spending has increased The recent US-Europe tensions have brought renewed focus to Europe’s military readiness and have reopened discussions regarding EU joint debt as a potential funding mechanism. The EU has already mutualized nearly €1trn of joint debt, but the likelihood this trend will continue has increased. That said, given restrictions in EU Treaties on using EU budget for military spending, a new loan programme is the only viable option. We believe there would be strong demand for EU defense loans based on the experience with SAFE. However, strong use of the EU to fund defense spending risks it becomes a victim of its own success, if its funding costs rise above EU sovereigns. Heightened US-Europe tensions reinvigorate discussion on more EU joint borrowing Tensions between Europe and the US intensified last weekend after US President Trump said he would impose new 10% tariffs starting 1 February on eight European countries (France, Germany, the UK, the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, and Finland) that temporarily sent troops to Greenland. These tariffs were set to increase to 25% in June and remain until a deal for the US to purchase Greenland was reached. These tariffs would have been in addition to the 15% tariffs agreed last July in the EU-US trade deal. records.text: An important caveat to our analysis so far is that policy shifts often involve important non-linearities. That is, the Governing Council can look through small and temporary deviations from the target but needs to respond to material and persistent deviations. This is especially true near the lower bound for interest rates (when policy is less effective) and for large shocks (which can lead to second-round effects, and thus more persistent deviations), as outlined in the ECB’s updated strategy. We therefore proxy for such non-linearities in two ways within our framework. One is to lower the responsiveness of growth to changes in the policy rate as a proxy for approaching the effective lower bound, where policy changes no longer affect growth. We see that the peak policy response is similar, but its persistence increases as transmission becomes weaker (Exhibit 6, grey line). The other is to increase the degree of persistence in the inflation process to proxy for stronger second-round effects in response to large shocks, as seen during 2022-23. Again, we find that the threshold for responding to deviations from the target falls and the peak policy response is larger (Exhibit 6, red line). records.text: M Global Foundation 6 Supply Outlook DM government bonds Across the G7, we expect net bond supply should amount to US$2.56 trillion in 2026, down 11% Y/Y, after central bank purchases, of which we expect none. Uncertainty over the future of fiscal policy across the G7 should keep investor expectations malleable and subject government bond markets to supply-related gyrations. We expect gross government bond supply (not including bills) to increase by US$76 billion in 2026 versus 2025 – representing a 10% Y/Y increase. After netting out redemptions, bond net issuance across the G7 should actually decrease by US$317 billion – amounting to a 11% Y/Y decrease. Net issuance decreases in the US, the euro area, Japan, and New Zealand. How should investors think about supply and its impact on price? Sovereign supply moves markets the most when expectations change for the sovereign supply outlook (see Between a Rock and a Hard Place, April 17, 2020). In 2026, surprises to the outlook for fiscal policy seem most likely to change expectations for the sovereign supply outlook. This means that bond yields can fall (rise) if investors come to expect less (more) supply than they thought before – even if that supply is more (less) than what they had to buy previously. For more, see our 2026 Global Macro Strategy Outlook, November 23, 2025. records.text: 23 January 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 39 Year-end haul for foreign investors in Treasury auctions Foreign demand for Treasuries seems to have resurfaced in a big way in December. Across all Treasury coupon auctions, the share of foreign and international allotments surged to high of 18%, substantially above the average of 11% in the preceding 12 months. Impressively, foreign allotments were robust across the board, except for the 2-year floater auction (which typically sees weaker foreign allotments compared to nominal and TIPS auctions). December marked the largest allocations to foreign investors since early 2022, just before inflation became a major concern and Treasury yields surged. Today’s chart shows the foreign allotments share against foreign official holdings of long-term Treasuries, reported in the Treasury TIC data. The two series generally line up with each other, possibly because foreign central banks and reserve managers tend to favor liquid benchmark Treasuries and accumulate them through auctions, whereas foreign private investors transact more frequently in off the off- the-runs in the secondary market. The latest available TIC data for November showed foreign official holdings remained around $3.5 trillion and without a notable trend in the past year. records.text: medium-term perspective, the latest events are likely to further reinforce the resolve for greater strategic autonomy in Europe. Whether this is achievable or not, European governments in general, and Germany in particular, are likely to try. This will involve further fiscal spending and therefore creates upside risks to fiscal policy and rates in Europe. Within Europe, countries with a weaker external position will be constrained, in particular the UK and France. However, France should benefit from its unique position in terms of defence within the EU and eurozone. This may limit the downside risks to OATs at a time at which the ability to tighten fiscal policy is constrained by domestic politics. For the US, we argued already that there are upside risks to fiscal policy into the midterms. However, it is worth noting that the US Treasury rates market does not price the weak external position of the US. We attributed that to the fact that US external debt is less “external” given its extra-territorial ability to de-facto access global private sector savings. This ability would be reduced if, amon g other things, Europe manages to regain some strategic autonomy. In terms of magnitude, a full pricing of the US external position would be consistent with UST10y being ~100bp higher on a cross-market basis. records.text: There are at least four arguments in favor of 2026 making a repeat of 2025, with IG and HY markets delivering positive excess returns despite the tight starting valuations. First, the macroeconomic picture remains benign, with above-trend US GDP growth, a Federal Reserve that is still in cutting mode, and cooling inflation. This is just the type of goldilocks environment, reminiscent of the 2004/05 and 2024 episodes, that should allow spreads to remain range-bound. Second, and as we have written about previously, the duration of both the IG and HY markets has come down dramatically since 2022 and currently sits near 10-year lows for IG and all-time lows for HY, which inherently lowers the risk to returns should some rebuild in spread premiums materialize. And third, corporate credit fundamentals remain strong, with leverage and coverage metrics improving across the board in Q3 earnings. Similarly, default risk remains subdued, which should keep the loss drag to credit returns to a minimum. Finally, we would point out that on a total return basis credit continues to screen well with all-in yields still trading around their 60th percentile for the IG index and 30th percentile for HY, which should continue to attract demand from total return investors. records.text: M Update 2 PCE Inflation Core PCE inflation rose 0.21% m/m in October and 0.16% in November, close to our expectation (consensus 0.2% for November, MSe 0.20% Oct and 0.18% Nov). September was slightly revised downward, -1bp. The October and November readings and our forecast for 0.46%m/m December are consistent with core PCE 3-month annualized inflation at 3.36% by December (2.67% in September), and the 6-month annualized pace at 3.01% (2.71% in September). The 12-month pace is expected to come at 3.07% in December (vs 2.83% in September). As expected, core goods prices moved sideways in October and November. Our comparison of goods more vs less exposed to tariffs suggests no clear tariff pass-through those two months. Note, however, that based on CPI data we expect goods more exposed to tariffs to continue the upward trend in December. Goods less exposed to tariffs should increase too, but mainly reflecting payback in computer software after months of weakness. Core services came in close to our forecast, slightly stronger than anticipated in October but softer in November. Core services ex-housing accelerated from the soft print in September, mainly due to acceleration in healthcare and financial services, two components that come from PPI and are, therefore, less affected by the shutdown noise. records.text: European Viewpoint | 23 January 2026 3 What would it mean for the ECB and the BoE? Absent a significant escalation that creates a large supply-side shock, the dominant effect from new US tariffs would be a spike in uncertainty – clearly a demand shock, as it would pose a major headwind to both investment and consumption, which are meant to drive the recovery throughout 2026. Some of the comments from ECB speakers in Davos would be consistent with this. The ECB could initially be reluctant to move quickly. However, beyond our current baseline, we think a persistent uncertainty shock without a major supply-side shock would end up leading the central bank to lower its Depo rate below the 1.75% we currently expect. Assuming the UK doesn’t retaliate, the weaker growth stemming from additional tariffs would likely be mildly disinflationary and encourage a dovish response from the BoE. However, if the UK does retaliate, it could imply a more ambiguous BoE response if reciprocal measures generate additional inflation pressures. Is this trade dispute different from developments seen throughout 2025? Again, while these tariffs are now off the table, the situation remains fluid, and they could easily come back. And if Europe were forced to respond, the stakes would be a lot higher. Why? Recent developments are proof that the US-EU agreement signed last year, as we argued back then, was never going to remove uncertainty. However, if underlying inflation proves to be stronger than we expect, belly forwards could reprice firmly above 2%, pushing 10-year yields toward the 2.5-3% range on a sustained basis. Such a fundamental reassessment could also cause the positive correlation between front-end forwards and the long-end of the curve to reassert itself as the market re-evaluates the risk of the BOJ falling behind the curve. This could exacerbate any country risk premia already in place, although it would also depend on how proactive the BOJ leans into the high inflation risks. Supply factors are another key consideration. We have previously shown that belly rates are the most sensitive to changes in free-float debt. Our supply projections suggest that the BOJ’s quantitative tightening (QT) will be a dominant factor driving up this free-float. While we do not expect the BOJ to alter its balance sheet policy despite the recent rise in yields, any surprise adjustment could significantly impact the 10-year segment of the JGB curve. As yields have risen, so has implied volatility in Japan, narrowing the gap with G3 volatility curves. This suggests JGBs are beginning to behave more similarly to other G4 markets, with vol risk premium also converging. records.text: , curves pivot steepened with EUR2s30s c.10bp steeper before flattening back as President Trump dropped his tariff threat on European nations following a framework deal being reached on Greenland. Amidst the crosscurrents that EUR rates found themselves in this week, the growth, inflation and monetary policy implications of renewed tariff risks for the EUR curve was in particular focus. As our economists discuss in Tariffs 3.0, Greenland-related developments pose more downside risks to the euro area and UK growth outlook, and will likely have a disinflationary impulse when taking into account all potential channels through which they would operate. Bundesbank President Nagel appeared to agree with this assessment as he stated in an interview that he is more concerned about economic growth than inflation in the wake of the fresh tariff threat and a reassessment of the ECB's monetary policy path might be needed. President Lagarde, in echoing her remarks from the December Governing Council meeting, argued that uncertainty has increased. On inflation, she stated that tariffs could cause a very small upward inflation effect, in line with Bank of France Governor Villeroy's remarks that trade tensions should have a muted inflation impact. Regarding Finland, we think a fresh negative outlook at Fitch's next review is relatively unlikely following the downgrade delivered last year. For S&P , the agency stated at its review last October, " we could consider a negative rating action in the next two years if Finland’s economic outlook significantly deteriorates compared with our expectations, leading to a pronounced and protracted deterioration in the country’s fiscal position" . With respect to Moody's, the agency stated, " downward pressure on the outlook, and ultimately the rating, could develop if the government did not deliver on its commitment to reverse the deterioration in fiscal metrics" . Given this commentary, we think the path of least resistance could be for these agencies to keep Finland's outlook at stable at their upcoming reviews, as they await more information on the economic/fiscal trajectory. We think these agencies may also take note of the cross-party debt brake agreement reached in the Finnish parliament last October, which aims to restrict budget deficits to 2.5% in future parliamentary terms. Nonetheless, fresh negative outlooks could still be a possibility in H2 if Finnish growth and fiscal data were to disappoint versus rating agency expectations. See our note here. The weekend after that a new trade war with Europe was threatened over US efforts to take ownership of Greenland from a NATO ally, Denmark. See our note here. records.text: m perspective, the latest events are likely to further reinforce the resolve for greater strategic autonomy in Europe. Whether this is achievable or not, European governments in general, and Germany in particular, are likely to try. This will involve further fiscal spending and therefore creates upside risks to fiscal policy and rates in Europe. Within Europe, countries with a weaker external position will be constrained, in particular the UK and France. However, France should benefit from its unique position in terms of defence within the EU and eurozone. This may limit the downside risks to OATs at a time at which the ability to tighten fiscal policy is constrained by domestic politics. For the US, we argued already that there are upside risks to fiscal policy into the midterms. However, it is worth noting that the US Treasury rates market does not price the weak external position of the US. We attributed that to the fact that US external debt is less “external” given its extra-territorial ability to de-facto access global private sector savings. This ability would be reduced if, among other things, Europe manages to regain some strategic autonomy. In terms of magnitude, a full pricing of the US external position would be consistent with UST10y being ~100bp higher on a cross-market basis. records.text: EUR corporate hybrids and AT1s: A defensive view on carry. EUR IG and HY spreads remain near record tights, keeping carry front and center. Corporate hybrid bonds and AT1s continue to stand out on relative value, with index spreads at 160bp and 295bp, respectively, even if both sit near the 1st percentile since 2010. Both markets have held up well through last year’s volatility despite a materially worse supply backdrop: net supply was up 7% for hybrids and 24% for AT1s vs. 3% for BB-rated senior unsecured bonds (Exhibit 10 and 11), underscoring the inflow-supported technical bid for EUR credit. Last week’s 6–12bp widening in hybrids and AT1 spreads (partly reversed since) was a useful reminder that “defensive” looks different across the two sectors. In corporate hybrids, dispersion was primarily quality-driven, with the lowest-rated issuers underperforming the most (Exhibit 12). In AT1s, call optionality was the key differentiator: the tightest-spread bonds widened the most as investors reassessed whether they were adequately compensated for extension risk (Exhibit 13). Going forward, we remain selectively overweight both sectors for carry, but favor a higher-quality tilt in corporate hybrids while gradually trimming exposure to the tightest AT1s bond spreads. Forward guidance remained unchanged, reiterating that rates will most likely be reduced in the course of 2026, but that the Committee is “not in a hurry” to ease. The outlook was little changed although the Committee put emphasis on inflation still being too high. The press conference focused heavily on geopolitical developments even though US tariffs were seen as having limited impact on Norway. Our economists continue to call for no Norges Bank cuts for the rest of the year (easing cycle resuming in March27), while markets are pricing in around 37bp of cumulative cuts. We think upcoming inflation prints will be key to der- mine Norges Bank’s future policy stance. We don’t see the case for a cut in March, for which also markets now price in little probability (~4bp). Uncertainty around funding and design is elevated and yields have surged in response. The BoJ delivered a somewhat hawkish hold this week. PM Takaichi has dissolved the lower house and called a general election for 8 February, looking to ride her high approval ratings to a stronger mandate. Meanwhile, the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP) – Japan’s largest opposition party – has formed a new party, the “Centrist Reform Alliance” (CRA), with Komeito, which had previously been in a coalition with the LDP , greatly increasing uncertainty surrounding the election outcome. Takaichi has added to her existing agenda of proactive fiscal measures for crisis management and growth investment by pledging to exempt food items from the consumption tax for a period of two years (Figure 1). This appears to be a counter-proposal to the CRA’s pledge to permanently eliminate that tax altogether. As Takaichi had consistently opposed consumption tax cuts since taking office, the move marks a significant policy reversal. Now all the political parties, in one form or another, are pledging consumption tax cuts, creating the impression of an election without a clear policy battleground. This was likely just for market color but could be an indication Treasury is thinking about a SOFR floater product, perhaps to limit increasing T-bills over a long horizon. We do not expect the liquidity of the 7y note to be materially improved by Treasury shifting to a quarterly cadence for the new issues. In fact, we think a larger gap between the on-the-run and off-the-run could expose the new issue auctions to additional volatility. The 7y auction, as of 2009, only tails about 51% of the time, however 23% of auctions tail more than 1bp. Fewer and larger CUSIPs could potentially aggravate an already volatile tenor. This conversion also presents the risk of the 7y new issue auctions becoming as volatile as the 30y new issue auctions (Figure 12). These 30y auctions, for instance, tend to tail more and have more volatility around the when-issued level compared to the 10y note. Looking back at previous auctions, the 30y new issue tails, on average, 1bp, with a standard deviation of 2.2bp. The 10y new issue, however, on average, tails only 0.6bp with a standard deviation of 1.4bp. This has us looking at the 5s10s spot curve today and thinking it has scope to steepen from here. Or in other words, off-the run 10y paper may roll into a much more crowded 7y sector than the market presently assumes. Figure 10. PM Takaichi has set the ruling coalition’s goal as securing a majority together with the Japan Innovation Pary (JIP), its coalition partner; however, her true objective is presumably a single- party majority for the LDP . Looking at the current composition of the 465-seat lower house by parliamentary group, the LDP holds 199 seats and JIP 34 (233 together as the ruling coalition), while the CDP holds 148 and Komeito 24 (172 for the CRA). Numerically, the LDP still exceeds the CRA. Yet simulations by the Asahi Shimbun based on results from the 2021 general election, where the LDP won decisively, suggest that under certain assumptions, the newly formed CRA could emerge as the largest party. However, it is important to note that this projection focuses solely on electoral-coordination scenarios and does not incorporate the current high approval rating of the Takaichi Cabinet (around 75%) or party support levels (according to the Nikkei: LDP 37%, JIP 7%, CDP 7%, Komeito 3%). M&A activity: Morgan Stanley Research anticipates a 20% rebound in global M&A in 2026 as equity markets heat up and regulators adopt a lighter touch on antitrust. This is good for equities - especially in the US where we are overweight - but a negative for corporate credit. In particular, our credit strategists pencil in ~$240bn of M&A-related gross issuance this year in the US. Fiscal deficit expansion: While markets have started pricing in higher term premia in part due to renewed fiscal concerns, we are more sanguine about actual supply risks for G4 government bonds. For Japan, a recent focal point of market jitters, our economics team believes the country's fiscal position is structurally improving, supported by the recovery in nominal GDP growth. Moreover, fiscal headlines are unlikely to translate one-for-one into materially higher market JGB issuance. Currency dynamics: We expect USD funding to become cheaper relative to local-currency funding, as our economics team anticipates further Fed easing in 2H26. In theory this should encourage non-US issuers to tilt issuers towards USD bonds issuance. However, funding costs for EM and Asian borrowers remain elevated in USD compared with G10 and local currency markets, suggesting non USD supply may rise instead. records.text: M Global Foundation 18 US ABS Consumer ABS supply should decline in 2026 after four straight years of growth, coming in at $242bn. We expect issuance to be down ~7% y/y as auto lenders tighten or maintain tight underwriting standards amid consumer-health concerns (especially low-to-middle income). Lower expected auto sales in 2026 versus 2025 - driven by tariffs and some pull- forward of 2025 demand ahead of policy-linked price increases - should further weigh on auto ABS. With our US Economics team forecasting a slowing rate of spending growth as consumers pull back, we expect gross issuance to retreat from all-time highs and net issuance to fall by half. Weakness in autos and cards should be partly offset by stronger unsecured consumer issuance, with increased BNPL activity a tailwind. Commercial ABS issuance should grow in 2026, with gross issuance forecast at ~$117bn and net issuance at ~$43bn, led by digital infrastructure and supported by growth in other commerical subsectors. While net issuance abated in 2025 in the non-digital infrastructure portion of commercial ABS, we expect a reversion to the mean in 2026, partly due to the rate cuts we anticipate. Data centers remain a key supply driver: we expect $24bn of data center issuance in 2026, up from $15bn in 2025. Fiber was the brightest spot of the ABS complex in 2025, with gross issuance up >125%, driven by the entry of enterprise fiber players who account for over half of issuance. THEME OF THE WEEK: EM RESILIENCE As markets digest the risk events stemming from the US’s renewed interest for Greenland and the sudden turbulence in Japan’s bond market, DMFX volatility has risen sharply, reflecting the fact that the latest shocks originated in developed markets. Thus far, most of the volatility has been concentrated in DM, with EMFX showing an uptick , but to a much smaller degree , resulting in a widening EM -DM volatility gap as investor risk sentiment retraced. EM resilience during global risk-off episodes is not new; we saw a similar pattern last year following “Liberation Day,” as EM outperformed thanks to stronger bala nce sheets, improved external positions, still -light positioning, and a weaker dollar. These fundamental factors remained intact, and as long as the global growth outlook stays benign, the positive case for EM should remain in place. On the weaker side, we expect volatile Irish growth to contribute negatively to the area-wide print, which we forecast at +0.2%qoq on a rounded basis, although uncertainty remains elevated. In our view, a lot of this is just political headlines. Both federal states are governed by political parties which support the policy of the central government – which, to a large extent, cause the financial challenges for the federal states. The financial equalization scheme can only be adjusted by a two-thirds majority in the German parliament. Moreover, significantly reducing the number of federal states as proposed by Bavaria seems impossible, as it contradicts the so-called “eternity guarantee” regarding the existence of federal states stipulated in Art 79 Grundgesetz, the German Basic Law. Overall, the 2025 numbers regarding the German financial equalization scheme between federal states confirm our view that all federal states should be rated equally (and in line with Bunds), as in the case of Fitch, currently at AAA. Services inflation fell back to 3.4% YoY (3.5% prev.) supported by easing price pressures in recreation, especially accommodation and package holidays. Core goods inflation was confirmed at 0.4% YoY, down 0.1pp from November. The full inflation breakdown confirmed extensive weakness across the goods basket. We continue to expect headline HICP to drop below the 2% target in Jan-26, to 1.6- 1.7% YoY. Negative base effects from energy will dominate, although the recent rally in commodity prices have pushed our forecast slightly up compared to the end of last year (when we were expecting 1.5-1.6%). Crude oil has increased c.7% over the month while gas has surged by almost 35%, driven by falling temperatures and relatively low storage levels. If sustained, these higher prices create some upside risks to our 2026 forecast (a 10% increase in gas prices could add c.0.1pp to headline inflation). records.text: Second part of report title FOCUS F O CU S 1 Iran scenarios: Power vacuum bigger energy worry than Hormuz constraint Revisiting Middle East escalation scenarios: Last year, we wrote that a severe escalation of tensions in the Middle East, with significantly disrupted oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz, could see both oil and gas prices reach triple- digit levels (see Global macro: Crude reality (3), dated 5 June). Given recent developments in Iran, we consider it timely to revisit our risk scenarios. Significant supply at risk: In an extreme escalation scenario, the Iranian regime may be backed into a corner and feel forced to deploy its strategic last resort: disrupting flows through the Strait of Hormuz. We consider this an unlikely scenario, but one which would deliver a very strong price response. About 15mbd of seaborne crude and around 20% of global LNG volumes transit daily through the Strait of Hormuz, meaning a severe disruption is always a concerning, if distant, risk. Kpler analysis suggests that the oil volumes at risk in a Hormuz closure are 9mbd – or about 9% of global demand – even if two pipelines that circumvent the Strait are full utilised to divert supply. This is very significant and explains why oil prices tend to rise sharply in scenarios where Hormuz may be severely constrained. Meanwhile, about 86 million tonnes of LNG, mainly from Qatar, would also be at risk, with limited diversion options, driving strong price upside in gas markets, too.

Update and the press conference. The December meeting minutes struck, in our interpretation, a dovish tone, with two members more or less explicitly raising the bar for hikes this year. Fresh information since the meeting has likely reinforced this perception, making an already high bar in policymakers’ minds appear even higher. Firstly, inflation fell notably short of the central bank’s forecast, with both CPIF and CPIF excluding energy printing at 2.1% and 2.3% y/y – some 0.4pp and 0.3pp below the Riksbank’s projections, respectively. Even if wary of the uncertainty surrounding the upcoming January inflation print – owing to price resets and changes in basket weights, which could materially alter the picture – the board will nevertheless likely take signal from the continued sharp appreciation of the Krona ( Figure 5). Importantly, SEK strength has continued to outpace the Riksbank’s own forecasts ( Figure 6), even against the backdrop of recent risk-off moves. In KIX terms, y/y appreciation has been at its fastest in at least a decade – one more factor that will likely contribute to keeping inflation low next year. 22 January 2026 46 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: The more things change...

Unless the tariffs are EU-wide (Trump has not said this so far), we believe the economic impact would be minimal for the region. The more relevant cost would likely come from a persistent spike in uncertainty, the magnitude of which would depend crucially on the size and duration of the shock. As a reminder, for Europe, a persistent one standard deviation jump in trade policy uncertainty (TPU) or economic policy uncertainty can cost up to 80bp of capex within a year. And both trade policy and general economic policy uncertainty are already clearly rising (Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4). For the UK, we previously estimated the direct hit from 10% tariffs on growth at 10- 15bps with a ~6-7% decline in goods exports to the US. But the cost of uncertainty and the indirect impact could be higher. Finally, any further escalation would add to those costs, depending on the type and size of that escalation. What would it mean for the ECB and the BoE? Absent a significant escalation that creates a large supply-side shock, the dominant effect would be a spike in uncertainty – clearly a demand shock, as it would pose a major headwind to both investment and consumption, which are meant to drive the recovery throughout 2026. The decree reflects the idea of redirecting the bulk of overseas resources into Colombia, mentioning the boost of infrastructure and other productive sectors as a key motivation. The government’s intention to change AFP’s investment regime has faced opposition from the AFP industry and from government officials who have opposed the move. How likely is the decree to be implemented? The decree implementation will be highly dependent on the outcome of the upcoming presidential election, in our view. Should there is a swing into the center-right/right, the new government is likely to either reverse the decree or to water it down in different ways (implementation timeframe, local and external caps, etc). Even though the intention of boosting different productive sectors could be well intended, in practice, it will take time to find ways to channel resources into different sectors and projects. records.text: tes. Even a stronger recovery would be unlikely to trigger early hikes, as the economy is far from any “overheating” scenario. Unemployment is elevated, and a period of sustained growth with slightly accommodative rates is likely needed to (1) absorb slack in the economy and (2) anchor inflation at target over the medium term. Hiking prematurely would risk sending the wrong signal to households and firms, with little clear benefit. A small rate recalibration (e.g., from 1.75% to 2.00%) cannot be fully ruled out if growth clearly and persistently exceeds expectations and if labour market improvements put 2027 inflation on a stronger trajectory than we currently foresee. For now, we maintain a flat rate path and see any potential hikes as a risk skewed toward 2027 rather than the year ahead.
